en: The Essential Meaning of the Vinaya’s Crucial Matters,
Compiled by the Dharma Master Deqi, a Bhikṣu of the Vinaya School at Baohua Mountain in Jinling,
Volume One.
The Yao Qin refers to the period during the reign of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin; it is called "Yao Qin" by the later ruler to distinguish it from other Qin dynasties.
It is selected to show that this is neither the Qin of the Ying clan following the Zhou, nor the Qifu Qin of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin, nor the Fu Qin of Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin;
thus, it is said to distinguish it from the "other Qin. As for the term "Ying Qin," [it refers to the former].
Regarding the term "Qin": during the time of Emperor Yao of the Qin ancestors, it was bestowed upon Bo Yi, who was granted the surname Ying.
Thus, he was called "Lao-Qin," which means "begging Qin. The title *Dharmakṣema* refers to the Qifu clan;
alternatively, it is said that "Qifo" (乞佛) is their clan name. They occupied Jincheng and Yuanchuan; Jincheng is an alternative designation for Lintao Prefecture in Shaanxi. Jincheng...
Yuanchuan was a courtesy name for Baoji County in Fengxiang Prefecture, Shaanxi. Yuanchuan styled himself Xiqin (Western Qin).
In the twelfth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, his name was Tanmouchen, also written as Tanmachen or Tanwuchen;
this translates as "Fafeng" (Abundance of the Dharma), a name given because his mastery of the Way and the Dharma was flourishing. He was from Central India.
He was a native of the Tu (Tuoba) people. As for those who speak of the Fu Qin dynasty: his surname was Fu, his given name was Jian, and his courtesy name was Yonggu.
He called himself the "Great Qin," and therefore it is known as the Fu Qin.
Sisi Temple means "succession.
Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), the first is the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*). "Grammar" (*śabda*) refers here to the science of teaching; it means being clear and lucid.
Because one thoroughly understands and masters all worldly methods of composition, calculation, and formal establishment, it is called the science of grammar.
Second, Hetuvidyā (Logic). *Hetu* refers to the causes for the arising of all phenomena.
This means that one thoroughly understands all worldly discourses, as well as scripts, seals, and insignia, and the causes of the ten thousand phenomena—earth, water, fire, and wind.
Therefore, it is called Hetuvidyā.
Third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*). "Medicine" refers to the methods of healing.

It means that one thoroughly understands all manner of worldly ailments—whether epilepsy, demonic poisons, imbalances of the four elements, curses by spirits and ghosts, or diseases of cold and heat—and masters their causes and their remedies; hence it is called the science of medicine.
Fourth, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*). "Art" (*śilpa*) refers to the craft of industry; "craftsmanship" (*karma*) refers to skillfulness.

This means being thoroughly proficient and masterful in all types of worldly skills and ingenuity, ranging from literary composition and poetic praise to the construction of cities, agriculture, commerce, various forms of music, divination, and the study of astronomy and geography.
Because one clearly understands and penetrates all such industrial arts and crafts, it is called the science of arts and crafts.
The fifth is inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*). "Inner" refers to the internal teachings of the Buddha-dharma.

This means using ethical discipline (*śīla*) to remedy the violation of precepts, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to remedy mental distraction, and wisdom (*prajñā*) to remedy ignorance; it extends to all various matters concerning defilement and purity, the erroneous and the correct.
Because one clearly understands and thoroughly penetrates the remedial methods for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it is called "Inner Science" (adhyātma-vidyā).
The character *mi* (靡) has the pronunciation *mi*; it means "none.
The character *zōng* (綜) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*); it refers to the loom shuttle used for weaving brocade. Although there may be ten billion threads of silk for the warp...
The character *wèi* (緯) is used here in the sense of "to guide" or "to draw forth.
*Xián* (閑) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). Mencius said, "He guarded the Way of the former sages.
*Bēng* (薨) is pronounced like *hōng*. When a Duke or Marquis dies, it is termed *bēng*.

*Ji* (pronounced like *ji*) means to dwell as a traveler or to be lodged elsewhere. It refers to being dependent on others. A minister who is a traveler by circumstance is fortunate if he merely receives pardon and leniency;
it does not mean he has been fully released.
*Lǔ* (pronounced like *lǔ*) means to plunder. To capture someone alive is called "plundering" (*lǔ*); to decapitate them is called "capturing" (*huò*).
*Zhēng* (pronounced like *zhēng*) means to verify.
*Wēi* (pronounced like *wéi*) means minute. One employs minute and subtle words so that the meaning does not fall into decline.
*Chí* (馳) means "to gallop. It refers to driving; when carriages and horses move swiftly, it is called *chí*. To run on horseback is termed *chí*. To urge on horses is termed *qū* (驅).
*Tuān* (脫湍) is pronounced as a voiced sound;
it is a term used for affirmation. *Jǐ* (幾) has the phonetic value of *jī*; "ji" refers to the subtle movement that is the first manifestation of good fortune.
*Dūn* (敦) is explained as *dūn* (墩); it means "thick" or "substantial. *Yù* (喻) has the phonetic value of *yú*; it denotes the appearance of speech being smooth and compliant.
When Zhao Zheng served as a Secretariat Librarian under Fu Jian of Former Qin, the foreign śramaṇas Saṃghabhūti and Dharmānanda entered Chang’an.
Zheng requested that Saṃghabhūti produce a Chinese translation of the *Vasumitra-sūtra* from its Sanskrit original.
Thereupon, Saṃghabhūti held the Sanskrit text while Zhu Fonian translated it into the language of Jin.
"Hongshi" refers to the Hongshi era of Later Qin. Later Qin was surnamed Yao; his name was Chang, with the courtesy name Jingmao.

A Qiang person from Chixiang, he served as the Dragon-Soaring General under Fu Jian of Former Qin. He led an attack against the Jin dynasty and later served as Grand Marshal (*simama*) to suppress the armies of Murong Rong, Shi Hu, and others.
Having been defeated, he fled in fear. At that time, the horse herders of Weibei and others incited five Qiang chieftains...
With more than ten thousand men, they enthroned Yao Chang as the leader of the alliance.

In the fourth month of the year Bingxu, the twelfth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty (387 CE), Yao Chang entered Chang’an from the Shaanxi region and ascended the imperial throne. He changed the era name to Jianchu and established the state title of Da Qin (Great Qin).
The Histories separate this from the Former Qin. On the *gengshen* day of the twelfth month in the eighteenth year of Taiyuan of the Jin dynasty (the *guisi* year), Chang died.
His son Xing ascended the throne and changed the era name to Huangchu. This lasted for five years. He then changed the era name again to Hongshi; thus it is called the Hongshi era of Later Qin.
The character for *ruò* (weak) is pronounced as *ruò*.

The term "weak-crown" (*ruòguàn*) refers to the age of twenty. *Tōng* means to penetrate; it is pronounced as *mǐn*, meaning sharpness of hearing. Thus, it signifies being thoroughly penetrating and acutely intelligent.
Regarding *gǔxùn*: *gǔ* is pronounced as *gǔ*. "Gǔxùn" refers to explaining the language of antiquity and the present to clarify their underlying causes.
*Yóu* (pronounced *yóu*) means "extreme" or "profound.

*Bèi* (pronounced *bì* in the upper tone) means "complete"; *guàn* (pronounced *guàn* in the lower tone) means "habitual practice. Thus, it refers to being fully equipped with and thoroughly practiced in local customs.
Xihe is the Fenzhou Prefecture in Shanxi Province. His courtesy name was Xihe.
"Qia" (洽) is pronounced like "xia" (狹); it means "to join.
"Zhuo" (著) is pronounced like "zhu" (注); it means "to clarify."

"Quality" (*zhì*) and "decisive" (*duàn*) form the compound *zhìduàn*. "Quality" (*zhì*) is pronounced with a departing tone; it means to examine or to verify. "Decisive" (*duàn*) is also pronounced with a departing tone; it means to resolve.
Together, they refer to examining, verifying, and resolving the meaning of the text.

"Yan-he": the upper character is pronounced yán; it means to exhaustively investigate and to thoroughly examine. The lower character is pronounced hé; it means to scrutinize so as to establish the reality [of the matter].
"Gòu" is pronounced gòu; it means to encounter. That is to say, to encounter illness.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains the eight winds as follows: obtaining things that are agreeable is called gain (*lābha*); losing things that are agreeable is called loss (*alābha*).
To be slandered behind one's back is called defamation (*nindā*); to be praised behind one's back is called praise (*praśaṃsā*). To be praised in one's presence is called fame (*yaśas*);

to be slandered in one's presence is called ridicule (*ayaśas*). That which afflicts the body and mind is called suffering (*duḥkha*); that which brings gratification to the body and mind is called pleasure (*sukha*).

Regarding the five methods for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-citta*): by practicing these five dharmas, afflictions are stilled, the mind becomes unmoving and undistracted, and various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are produced.

Because the mind is sustained by these dharmas of concentration, one enters and emerges from them with ease and stability; thus they are called "settling the mind. First, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) for sentient beings with excessive greed:
this refers to those who possess much lust and are mutually attached to the physical forms of men and women. One must...
One should counteract this by practicing the nine-fold contemplation of impurity, thereby ensuring that the mind of greedy attachment does not arise;
hence it is said: "For sentient beings with much greed, there is the contemplation of impurity."

2. The Contemplation of Compassion for Sentient Beings with Excessive Hatred: This refers to those who possess much anger and resentment, who immediately give rise to indignation toward objects that are disagreeable.

One should treat this with the contemplation of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*). By lovingly cherishing and feeling pity for all sentient beings, one does not give rise to a mind of hatred toward them;
hence it is called the "Compassion Contemplation for Those with Excessive Hatred."
3. Counting the Breath Meditation for Beings with Distracted Minds: This refers to those whose minds are excessively distracted;
they should employ the counting of breaths as a remedy. As for counting the breaths, one uses the inhalations and exhalations through the nostrils.

One may count either the exhalations or the inhalations, maintaining an upright mind and right mindfulness from one to ten—neither more nor less—repeating the cycle until the task is complete. This causes...
Because the mind is not distracted, it is said that for sentient beings with excessive distraction, one should practice the meditation on counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

Fourth, the meditation on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) for deluded sentient beings: this means that those who are ignorant and lack understanding should be treated by means of the meditation on causes and conditions.
As for the meditation on causes and conditions, it is the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination. This is because they are confused and inverted.

Denying cause and effect and clinging to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, one is led to contemplate these twelve links of dependent origination as a continuity through the three periods of time that is neither interrupted nor eternal,
thereby destroying the mind of ignorance; hence it is called "the contemplation of dependent origination for ignorant sentient beings."

5. Contemplation of Mindfulness of the Buddha for Sentient Beings with Many Obstacles: This refers to the fact that those whose obstacles are heavy should employ the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha to treat them.
There are three kinds of obstacles: First, the obstacle of dullness and mental obstruction.

One should contemplate the thirty-two marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (response body) Buddha, making each mark distinct and clear, thereby treating the dullness. Second, the obstacle of evil thoughts and reflections.
One should contemplate the Buddha of Recompense (Sambhogakāya) with its ten powers and four fearlessnesses to remedy this.

As for the obstacle of the oppression of the three realms, one should contemplate the Buddha of Dharma-nature (Dharmakāya), which is empty, quiescent, and unconditioned, to remedy it. Therefore, it is said: "Sentient beings with many obstacles practice the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha."
The mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*)—namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—is explained within the context of the eleven factors of the path.
As for mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*): when one contemplates the impurity of the body, then sensation, mind, and phenomena are also all impure.

When one contemplates that sensation is suffering, then body, mind, and phenomena are also all suffering. When one contemplates that the mind is impermanent, then body, sensation, and phenomena are also...
All are impermanent. Contemplating that phenomena are without self, one realizes that body, sensation, mind, and mental objects are likewise all without self.
One cultivates these four contemplations upon the four objects in order to destroy the perversions so that none remain.
The four preparatory practices are also called the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).

These four are collectively termed "preparatory practices" because when these practitioners seek to attain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—transforming from ordinary beings into noble ones—they give rise to the four mental states beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and cultivate the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

Using concentration as the support for wisdom and applying effort through practice, these are called the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*). The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) corresponds to the first fruit, the *srotāpanna*.
First, the preparatory stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*): "Heat" is named after a metaphor; it refers to how a person drills wood to produce fire. Fire...

Although one has not yet emerged [from the outflows], one first attains the sign of "warmth. This is like using the fire of wisdom within this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) to burn the fuel of afflictions;
although one has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one has already attained the precursor to the fire of wisdom, and is therefore called "warmth."
Regarding the preparatory practice (*prayoga*): "untainted" (*anāsrava*) means not falling back into the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
Second, the preparatory practice of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*). "Summit" refers to the observation-practice (*vipaśyanā*) becoming increasingly clear;

it stands above the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*), like reaching the peak of a mountain from which one gazes in all four directions and perceives everything with complete clarity. Thus, it is called the preparatory practice of the summit. As for "gazing in all four directions": [it refers to the observation of the four truths].
This refers to the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the preparatory stage of the three patiences (*kṣānti*), there are two meanings for "patience": first, the sense of "affirmation" (*saṃpratyaya*).

This means that within this stage, one is able to affirm the principle of the Four Noble Truths; that is, the truth of suffering is indeed suffering, and so on, up to the truth of the path being indeed the path.

This is the path. Second is the meaning of "certainty" (*niyata*), which means that these roots of goodness are certain not to regress; therefore, it is called the preparatory stage of patience (*kṣānti-prayoga*).

Fourth is the preparatory stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma-prayoga*): this refers to the stage wherein one contemplates the principles of the Four Noble Truths, though one has not yet realized them.
Because it is the most supreme within the world, it is called the "Highest Mundane Preparatory Practice" (*laukikāgradharma*).

"Vehicle" (*yāna*) has the meaning of "transporting. This means that the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas each take their respective Dharma as a vehicle to transport themselves out of the birth and death of the triple world and arrive together at the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness; therefore, they are called the "Three Vehicles."
The "three realms" refer to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. *Nirvāṇa* in Sanskrit means "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*) in the Chinese language.
First, the Vehicle of the Śrāvaka: they attain awakening to the Way by hearing the Buddha’s teachings; hence they are called "Hearers. This refers to their...
One knows suffering, abandons its origin, aspires toward its cessation, and cultivates the path; therefore, these Four Noble Truths constitute the vehicle (*yāna*). The Four Noble Truths are:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Second is the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle: because one awakens to the principle of the true reality by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, it is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
This means first contemplating from ignorance as the condition up to old age and death; this is the contemplation of the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Next, contemplating from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death; this is the contemplation of the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination.

By contemplating this cessation of dependent origination, one realizes that there is neither arising nor cessation; it is by means of these twelve links of dependent origination that one takes as the vehicle.
The twelve links of dependent origination are: first, ignorance; second, volitional formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form;
fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation; eighth, craving; ninth, clinging; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth; and twelfth, old age and death.
Third, the Bodhisattva Vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*). "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term; its full form is *bodhisattva*.
In the language of China, it means "enlightened sentient beings," referring to one who awakens all sentient beings.

Because Bodhisattvas practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) to extensively transform sentient beings so that they may transcend birth and death, these six perfections constitute the vehicle. As for the six perfections:
First, generosity; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, meditative concentration; and sixth, wisdom.
Regarding the three types of knowledge, the first is "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*): this refers to all internal phenomena. "Internal" means that which can be known and understood.

All external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) and their external names can also be known and understood; this is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), which refers to the wisdom of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

Regarding internal phenomena (*adhyātmadharma*) and internal names: these refer to the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) expounded within the [Buddhist] principle (*nyāya*) and the names that express them.
Since the Buddha’s teachings are spoken in reliance upon this principle, they are termed "within the principle" (*nyāyāntara*). External phenomena and...
"Name" refers to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) that are expressed beyond [the nature of] reality, as well as the words that express them.
Because non-Buddhists and others contravene reality through arbitrary conceptualization, they are said to be "beyond reality."

Second is the Knowledge of the Aspects of the Path (*mārgākārajñatā*). This refers to the ability to employ all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas to give rise to all the seeds of goodness in sentient beings;
this is called the Knowledge of the Aspects of the Path, which is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva.
Third is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*): that which is able, by means of the knowledge of all modes, to know all paths and to know all aspects;
this is called the knowledge of all modes, which is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha.

Regarding the "Three Truths" (*trīṇi satyāni*): "Truth" (*satya*) means to examine with precision. It refers to examining all phenomena with precision as being simultaneously empty (*śūnya*), provisionally existent (*prajñapti-sat*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Being simultaneously empty is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); being simultaneously provisionally existent is the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and being simultaneously the Middle Way is the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).

When these three are distinct and sequential, they constitute the sequential Three Truths; when the three and the one are mutually unimpeded, they constitute the perfectly interfused Three Truths. [The text here marks a section break.]
"Successive" means that the three truths do not interpenetrate one another. "Gradual" means that truth comes first, the conventional second, and the middle third;

this is the three truths of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao). "Perfectly Interfused" means that raising one is immediately all three, and the entirety of the three is one; this is the three truths of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).

First, the True Truth (*satya*): "True" refers to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which means the sublation of all phenomena. For all dharmas are fundamentally empty, yet sentient beings do not realize this;
they grasp them as real and thereby give rise to deluded views. If one uses the contemplation of emptiness to wash away these [views], [delusion is eliminated].
This is what is called the reality of things. When one spontaneously forgets emotions and forgets even that forgetting, one is then able to transcend all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one transcends them, the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is naturally and clearly realized; therefore, it is named the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
Second, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Conventional" refers to the mundane world; it is the designation for the establishment of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Although all phenomena are fundamentally empty and ultimately ungraspable, if one contemplates them through the perspective of provisional designation (*upāya*), one can clearly and thoroughly realize that their nature is inherently complete.
Thus, all phenomena appear distinctly and vividly; therefore, it is called the conventional truth.
Regarding the "Middle Truth among the Three": "Middle" refers to the central mean, which signifies the unification of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

All phenomena are fundamentally neither separate from the two extremes nor identical with them. If one observes them through the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), then one can truly comprehend all phenomena as being neither ultimate (*paramārtha*) nor conventional (*saṃvṛti*), yet both ultimate and conventional. They are pure and transparently penetrating, perfectly integrated and unimpeded—this is "oneness."
It is three, yet it is one within those three; because it is inconceivable, it is called the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).
The *Vedamāṇḍikya Sūtra* states: "In the beginning, the person Brahmā created one Veda.
Subsequently, there was a ṛṣi named Śuci who transformed the one into four; therefore, they are called the Four Vedas. In the Sanskrit language, "Veda" [is so called]. In the Chinese language...
Regarding the *Jñānakāṇḍa* (Discourse on Knowledge): this refers to the heterodox treatises composed by the Brahmins.

Using worldly wisdom, they authored books on the cultivation of life and other subjects, which are divided into four distinct categories; therefore, they are called the Vedas. These texts have never been transmitted to the Eastern Land (China).
One *āyu*. In Sanskrit it is *āyu*; in the language of China, it means "the span of life" (*fāngmìng*) and is also called "nourishing longevity" (*shòuyǎng*).
It is a book for cultivating and refining one's nature. "Cultivating" (*shàn*) means to rectify or govern.
2. *Sūtra* (Sanskrit: *sūtra*). This term has no equivalent translation [in Chinese]. It refers to books concerning sacrifices and prayers.

3. *Vyākaraṇa* (Sanskrit: *vyākaraṇa*). This term has no equivalent translation [in Chinese]. It refers to books concerning ritual etiquette, divination, military strategy, and the deployment of troops.
The four *ādarśa*. In the Sanskrit language, *ādarśa* has no equivalent translation [in Chinese]. It refers to treatises on various arts, skills, incantations, and medical prescriptions.
*Miao* (pronounced *mǎo*) means a vast expanse of water.

"Exhaustively detailed" (*xiang-xi*): "detailed" (*xiang*) means complete; "exhaustively" (*xi*) means to the end, or to know thoroughly. Does this mean that I am complete, detailed, and possess exhaustive knowledge?
The *Ratnakaṇḍa* (如意珠) is also called *maṇi*, or sometimes *yuma*; its correct name is *maṇi*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
It is like a maṇi jewel: if it is placed among six different colors, it takes on whichever single color is present. If wrapped with a blue object, the water becomes blue;
if wrapped with yellow, red, white, crimson, or pale green, it takes on those respective colors, such as yellow and so forth. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Ānanda asks Kauśika:
"Is this maṇi jewel a celestial treasure, or is it a real thing from Jambudvīpa? Śakra replied: [It is a celestial treasure].
Śakra-devānām-indra said: "This is a treasure of the heavens; people of Jambudvīpa also possess such treasures, but their marks of merit are slight and incomplete.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Some say this jewel emerges from within the brain of the Dragon King.
If a person obtains this jewel, poison cannot harm them, and they will not be burned when entering fire. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "It is also said that it is like..."
The term *cintāmaṇi* appears to differ between the Chinese and Sanskrit traditions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* seem to list them as two distinct names side by side.
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* mentions a *maṇi* jewel as large as a kneecap, whereas the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *cintāmaṇi* is shaped like a mustard seed.
Furthermore, it says that the *cintāmaṇi* originates from the Buddha’s *śarīra*; if the Dharma were to perish...
When [the relics] are exhausted, all the śarīras transform into cintāmaṇi jewels. The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha* (Guanjing) refers to the cintāmaṇi as a maṇi.
Tiantai says: "Maṇi means 'as one wishes' (*yìrúì*)."
*Yu* (pronounced yù): to stop; to resist. *Líng* (pronounced líng):
to violate. *Bò* (pronounced pò):
the dark portion of the moon's body is called *bò*; furthermore, *bò* refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance...
When [the afflictions] are exhausted, delusion is forgotten.
"Yi" (宜) should be pronounced as "ni" (倪); it means "to accord with principle. This refers to the meaning of "according with reality" (*yathābhūta*).
This is explained in detail among the bhikṣus who have destroyed the fetters within the nine realms.
The desires of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are precisely sensual desires. Among them, the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) take physical union as their desire;

the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven takes wind as their desire; the Yāma Heaven takes embracing as their desire; the Tuṣita Heaven takes holding hands as their desire; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven takes gazing and smiling as their desire;
and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven takes merely gazing as their desire. They are called "heavenly" (*deva*) because they...

However, because their natural pleasures, superior bodies, and supreme excellence differ, and because they are also called "most excellent" and "radiant," they are named the Six Heavens of Desire according to these differing desires.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings is forty thousand *yojanas* above the human realm; each *yojana* being forty *li*.
They dwell upon the slopes of Mount Sumeru and the peaks of the seven golden mountains, at the same level as the sun and moon. There are four kings of these heavens:

the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East dwells on the golden terrace of Mount Sumeru and presides over the hosts of *gandharvas*; the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka of the South... [dwells on the silver terrace and presides over the hosts of *kumbhāṇḍas*].
The Heavenly King [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] dwells upon the lapis lazuli terrace of Mount Sumeru and presides over the host of kumbhāṇḍas.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the West dwells upon the silver terrace of Mount Sumeru and presides over the host of nāgas.

The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa of the North dwells upon the crystal terrace of Mount Sumeru and presides over the host of yakṣas; he governs all malevolent spirits and ghosts, ensuring they do not dare [to cause harm].

Because they subdue [the asuras] who ravage [the world], they are named "World-Protectors" (Lokapāla). The four kings together with their retinues are collectively called the Four Heavenly Kings (Cāturmahārājika).

This is the result induced by the superior grade of the ten virtuous actions (daśakuśala), or the result induced by the predominant merit of the precept against killing, or the power induced by the observance of the fast (upavāsa) for one day and one night. Their bodies are seventy-five *zhang* tall. By means of human...
Fifty intermediate kalpas constitute one day and night for them, and their lifespan is five hundred years. Calculated by human reckoning, this amounts to nine million years;
however, there are also those who die prematurely. At the time of death, the five signs of decay appear:
first, the flowers on the head wither; second, sweat exudes from the armpits; third, the clothing becomes soiled and stained; fourth, the body emits a foul odor; fifth, [the body loses its luster].
The original seat of pleasure:
the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is eighty thousand *yojanas* above the human realm and resides upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;
"Trāyastriṃśa" is a term from the Sanskrit language, which translates here as the "Heaven of the Thirty-three. This refers to the four sides of the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Each [of these] has eight heavens, which stand in parallel rows, making thirty-two; together with Śakra, the Heavenly King in the center, they constitute the thirty-three [devas].
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "In the past, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan."
Together with thirty-two companions, they collectively cultivated merit and virtue. At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru;
Kauśika became the Heavenly King, each of them becoming a Śakra-devendra, and the thirty-two companions became his ministers.
This, too, was the result of the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action, or specifically the predominant merit of the two precepts against killing and stealing.
This is brought about by the power of a single day and night of fasting. The bodies of the devas are all one hundred and fifty *zhang* in height;
only the body of Śakra is three hundred *zhang*, due to his having extensively cultivated the karma of reverence in the past.
One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for them, and their lifespan is one thousand years. Calculated by human reckoning, this is three... [years].
For sixteen million years, there are premature deaths and the manifestation of the five signs of decay, as previously described;
the same should be understood to apply to all subsequent heavens. In Sanskrit, he is called Kauśika, also known as Śakra Devānām Indra;
in the language of China, he is called "Nengtiān" (Capable Lord of Heaven). The term "Dishi" (Śakra) combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit designations.
The Yāma Heaven is eighty thousand yojanas above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas above the human realm.
In the midst of space, there is a ground like a cloud that remains brilliantly stable; this constitutes the Yāma Heaven.
This is translated as "Time-Portion" (Yāma), because its inhabitants constantly proclaim joy at every moment. They distinguish day from night by the opening and closing of lotus flowers.
Night. This is the result of the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), combined with the practice of seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

Alternatively, it is the result of the superior merit of the three precepts—abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—or likewise the merit of the eight or ten precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*, *daśa-śīla*).
His body is two hundred and twenty-five *zhang* tall; [in this realm], two hundred years of the human world constitute one [unit of time].
The lifespan there is two thousand celestial years, day and night.
The Tuṣita Heaven is one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas above the Yāma Heaven and three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas above the human realm.
In the midst of space, it exists like a cloud; its ascent is subtle and refined, and it does not descend to the lower realms.
The realms of humans and devas constitute the Tuṣita Heaven; this is translated as "Contentment.
This means that while the Yāma Heaven excessively enjoys the exquisite pleasures of the five desires of the desire realm and does not know contentment, this heaven is able to be content.

This is the result of the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade, obtained through the attainment of subtle abiding, or perhaps through an increase in the sevenfold precepts consisting of the three bodily and four verbal actions.
This is brought about by superior merit, or perhaps by the power of the eight precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth. His body is three hundred *zhang* tall.
Four hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night there; his lifespan in that heaven is four thousand years. As for the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), they are:
the desire for forms, the desire for sounds, the desire for fragrances, the desire for tastes, and the desire for tactile sensations. As for "subtle abiding," it refers to the six subtle gates.
This is the first of the four methods for cultivating contemplation within the gates. One spontaneously awakens to the dissolution of body and mind;
entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one perceives neither internal nor external appearances. The dharma of concentration sustains the mind, which remains naturally unmoving.

Within this state of concentration, one uses the "mind-eye" to clearly contemplate the subtle signs of the inhalation and exhalation within this body; therefore, it is called attaining both [gross and] subtle abiding.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven is 320,000 yojanas above the Tuṣita Heaven and 640,000 yojanas above the human realm.
In the midst of space, there is ground like clouds that transcends the lower realms; one is able to manifest transformations therein.
Because they delight by personally creating the five sensory objects of desire, it is called the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. This is the upper [part].

They practice the ten wholesome deeds (*daśakuśala*) and, further accomplishing the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they obtain a body one hundred and seventy-five *zhang* in height.
With eight hundred human years constituting one day and night, their lifespan in that heaven is eight thousand years.
As for the "five objects" (*pañca-viṣaya*), these are the objects of form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), fragrance (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), and touch (*spraṣṭavya*).
The Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) is six hundred and forty thousand yojanas above the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
It is one million two hundred and eighty thousand yojanas above the human realm. In the midst of space, there is ground like clouds;

by making use of the transformations produced by others, they accomplish their own pleasures. Therefore, it is named "Mastery over the Transformations of Others. This is the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), accomplished in conjunction with [the other levels].
The body length produced by the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the concentration of the stage not yet arrived at) is four hundred and fifty *zhang*.
One thousand six hundred human years constitutes one day and night there; the lifespan in that heaven is sixteen thousand years.
The gods of the realm of form and the realm of formlessness possess the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
the gods of the formless realm possess only the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The Brahmakāyika devas transcend the six heavens of the desire realm; because they are far removed from the three afflictions of food, drink, and sexual desire, as well as sleep, they are called "Brahma.
"Brahma" signifies that which is pure and free from defilement. Generally speaking, all four dhyānas are termed Brahma-heavens, for they are all pure.
Specifically speaking, it is in the first dhyāna that one first becomes free from the defilement of desire.

It alone receives the name "Brahma. The *Mahābuddhōṣṇīṣa-sūtra* states: "When attachment does not arise and there is no lingering in the desire realm, such a person, by virtue of this thought, becomes a companion of Brahmā and is named a member of the Brahmakāyika Heaven (Brahma-parṣadya). Their lifespan is twenty minor kalpas, and their body is half a yojana in height."

The *Brahmapurohita-mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra* states: "When the habit-energies of desire have been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests, one takes delight in and accords with all forms of discipline (*vinaya*).
Such a person is able to practice the virtues of Brahmā at that time and is named a Brahmapurohita.
Their lifespan is forty minor kalpas, and their body is one yojana in height."

The *Mahābrahmā Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra* states: "If one’s body and mind are wondrously perfect, one’s dignified deportment is flawless, and one possesses pure precepts augmented by clear awakening, such a person shall, at that time, be able to lead the Brahma assembly and become a Great Brahma King.
His lifespan shall be sixty minor kalpas, and his body shall measure half a yojana."

The gods of the Heaven of Limited Light—regardless of whether they are among humans, in the heavens, in the desire realm, or in the first dhyāna—abide neither in nor cling to the samādhi of non-applied thought and sustained observation alone;
with single-minded diligence, they seek advancement and have newly attained the samādhi of neither applied thought nor sustained observation.
He enters the second dhyāna. Because the power of this dhyāna is profound, at the end of his life he is reborn among the Parīttābha (Limited Light) devas.

This is what the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* refers to as "the mind being clear and unmoving, from which a tranquil depth gives rise to light. The calamity of fire does not reach there, and his lifespan is one great kalpa.

The body is two yojanas in height. From the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, all are termed the samādhi of non-discursive thought and non-discursive investigation.
Among the gods of the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, one repeatedly practices the power of the second dhyāna; upon the end of life, one attains rebirth there.

This deva is what the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa Sūtra* refers to as "light shining upon light, illuminating without end, reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and universally becoming lapis lazuli.
His lifespan is four great kalpas, and his body is four yojanas in height.

The Ābhāsvara devas are the supreme among celestial beings; through their profound entry into the power of the second dhyāna and their concurrent cultivation of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they attain birth in this heaven upon the end of their lives.

As stated in the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra*, they "sustain the perfect radiance," accomplish the essence of the teaching, manifest pure transformations, and apply themselves with inexhaustible utility. Their lifespan is eight great kalpas, and their bodies are eight yojanas in height.
As for the Śuddhāvāsa deities, they do not dwell among humans or in the heavens above. The Brahmakāyika and Ābhāsvara deities merely abide in and are not attached to the second dhyāna;
with single-minded diligence, those who first realize the third dhyāna are reborn in this heaven immediately upon the end of their lives.
They are not reached by calamities of water. Their lifespan is sixteen great kalpas, and their height is sixteen yojanas.
Having cultivated the power of the third dhyāna for immeasurable kalpas, beings of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven pass away and are reborn in this heaven;
their lifespan is thirty-two great kalpas, and their height is thirty-two yojanas.
The Śubhakṛtsna devas enter deeply into the power of the third dhyāna and concurrently cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Upon the end of their lives, they are reborn in this heaven. Their lifespan is sixty-four great kalpas, and their bodies are sixty-four yojanas in height.
Regarding the Heaven of the Birth of Merit (Puṇyaprasava), whether among humans or in the heavens of the first, second, or third dhyānas,

those who do not savor or become attached to the third dhyāna, but instead apply themselves with single-minded diligence and newly realize the fourth dhyāna, will, at the end of their lives, be reborn in this heaven.
The retribution is subtle and wondrous; palaces follow the body, and even the ground like clouds is not required.
For this reason, it is also called the Heaven Without Clouds (*Anabhraka*) in other sūtras. Neither of the three calamities can reach it.
The lifespan is one hundred and twenty-five great kalpas, and the body is one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in height.
Through the power of having cultivated the fourth dhyāna during his time among the Puṇyaprasavā devas, he was reborn in this heaven at the end of his life.
His lifespan is two hundred and fifty great kalpas, and his body is two hundred and fifty yojanas in height.
The gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*) enter deeply into the power of the fourth dhyāna and concurrently cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Upon the end of their lives, they are reborn in this heaven, where their lifespan is five hundred great kalpas and their bodies are five hundred yojanas in height.
The beings of the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva) were among humans and gods who, having embraced the false teachings of non-Buddhist outsiders, became weary of coarse ideation.
Through the power of repeated cultivation, they suppressed and removed the defiled attachment of the desire realm and the first three dhyānas.

Relying upon the fourth dhyāna, they extinguished the mental states and mental factors of the preceding six consciousnesses, causing them not to manifest. Because the cessation of ideation is primary, it is called "non-conception."
He attains this concentration. Having attained it, he does not fall away nor lose it; at the end of his life, he is immediately reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
His lifespan is also five hundred great kalpas, and his body is also five hundred yojanas in height.

Regarding the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*), within this homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness in the fourth dhyāna, there are further these five [levels].

This is the abode where Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), who are noble ones having attained the third fruit and have severed the defilements of the four lower stages but have not yet severed the defilements of the higher stages, reside.
As for the first, No Affliction, it is produced by the inferior grade of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*).

This means that after the practitioner has first entered the fourth dhyāna, within this meditative absorption, they first give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of untainted (anāsrava) mind manifesting before them;
next, they give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of tainted (sāsrava) mind manifesting before them;
and again, they give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of untainted mind manifesting before them. In this manner, they gradually reduce [the number of moments] until only two remain.
When two moments of the outflowing (sāsrava) and two moments of the non-outflowing (anāsrava) arise, this is called the completion of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of mixed cultivation.
Next, one moment of the non-outflowing and one moment of the outflowing arise; this single moment of the non-outflowing is called the completion of the fundamental stage (*maula*).

By employing the non-outflowing to intermingle with and perfuse the outflowing, the form-sphere concentration (*rūpadhyāna*) becomes increasingly clear and its karmic fruition becomes increasingly superior. Through this, it serves as a support for...
Due to their past karma, after the end of their lives they were reborn in this heaven. Their lifespan is one thousand great kalpas, and their bodies are one thousand yojanas in height.
They only progress upward and never regress. Upon encountering even a single instance of the word "Buddha," they immediately transcend the realm of dust and become arhats.
Regarding the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapa*), the "two [aspects of] no heat" are the result produced by the medium grade of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*).

Taking the three preceding moments of the fundamental lower grade as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one further induces one moment of untainted (*anāsrava*) and one moment of tainted (*sāsrava*) mind.
With these three moments of untainted mind as the fundamental basis, one is sustained by this prior karma and is thus born in this heaven, where the lifespan is two thousand [years].
The Great Kalpa. Their bodies are two thousand yojanas in height.
As for the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa), "Good Vision" refers to that which is induced by the mixed cultivation of the superior grade; it employs the preceding six mental states.
All these constitute the preliminary application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, by inducing three minds as the fundamental basis and utilizing their past karma, they attain birth in this heaven.
Their lifespan is four thousand great kalpas, and their bodies are four thousand yojanas in height.
Regarding the four classes of Śubhakṛtsna gods: they are produced by the mixed cultivation of superior grades.

Using the preceding nine moments of mind as preparatory applications (*prayoga*), one further induces three moments of mind as the fundamental [meditative states] to support their prior karma, thereby attaining birth in this heaven.
Their lifespan is eight thousand great kalpas, and their bodies are eight thousand yojanas in height.
Regarding the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Heaven of Ultimate Form): it is produced by the highest grade of mixed meditative cultivation (*miśraka-dhyāna*).

Using the previous twelve moments of mind as preparatory application (*prayoga*), one further induces three moments of mind as the fundamental [meditation] to support that prior karma, thereby attaining birth in this heaven.
Its lifespan is sixteen thousand great kalpas, and its body is sixteen thousand yojanas in height.
Ten days.

As for the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), regardless of whether they are among humans or in the heavens of the first, second, third, or fourth dhyānas—excluding only the gods of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) and the five types of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*)—if any others who have cultivated the concentration of the sphere of infinite space achieve its perfection, their life... [ends].
Upon the end [of their previous life], they are born in this heaven. Since they lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it cannot be said that they have a location with spatial dimensions;
rather, their abode consists solely of the boundless space perceived by the subtle sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Their lifespan is forty thousand great kalpas.

As for the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), regardless of whether they belong to the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, or the Sphere of Infinite Space, they cultivate only the meditative absorption of the sphere of consciousness.

Upon the completion of their lives, they are reborn in this heaven. Their abode consists solely of the infinite mental consciousness as perceived by the subtle sixth consciousness. Their lifespan is forty thousand great kalpas.

As for the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana), regardless of whether they belong to the Desire Realm or the Form Realm, they are born in this heaven immediately upon the end of their lives simply by accomplishing the meditative concentration of the Sphere of Nothingness.
Their abode consists solely of the subtle objects perceived by the sixth consciousness, which are neither space nor consciousness. Their lifespan is sixty thousand great kalpas.
The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) does not depend on the two realms of desire and form, nor on the three stages such as emptiness;
rather, it is accomplished solely by cultivating the meditative absorption of Neither Perception nor Non-perception. Upon the end of life, one is reborn in this heaven.
Its locus consists solely of an extremely subtle object of perception for the sixth consciousness—a realm that is neither existent nor non-existent. Its lifespan is eighty thousand great kalpas.
It dwells at the very summit of the three realms of existence, beyond which there is nothing further to advance.

In the language of the Brahmins, it is called Pūrvavideha; in the language of China, it is translated as "Victorious Body" (Shengshen), because its inhabitants possess bodies superior to those of the southern continent.
It is also translated as "First," meaning that the sun first rises from here. It is situated to the east of Mount Sumeru.
That land is narrow in the east and broad in the west, shaped like a half-moon. It is nine thousand yojanas in width. The faces of its inhabitants are likewise shaped like a half-moon.
The human body is eight cubits tall, and the lifespan is two hundred and fifty years. In Sanskrit it is called Sumeru;
in the language of China, it is translated as "Wondrous High" (Miaogao).
Jambudvīpa is called *Jambudvīpa* in the Sanskrit language; in the vernacular (Chinese) it means "Superior Gold. Regarding the *jambu* tree:
*dvīpa* is the name for the continent, which is named after the tree, hence it is called Jambudvīpa. It lies to the south of Mount Sumeru.

Its land is narrow in the south and broad in the north, shaped like a carriage box (*śakaṭa*). It measures seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise shaped like the land.

As for their physical form and lifespan, there is no fixed limit. At the beginning of the kalpa’s formation, the lifespan was immeasurable; at the end of the kalpa of decrease, it does not exceed ten years;
and at the peak of the kalpa of increase, it reaches eighty-four thousand years. At present, the human lifespan does not even reach one hundred years, and many die prematurely.

Therefore, regarding the retribution of karmic results, they do not equal those of the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha), let alone those of the two continents to the northwest (Aparagoyānīya and Uttarakuru). Nevertheless, there are...

In three respects, they surpass even the various devas, let alone those of the Northern Continent: first, they are able to sever sexual desire; second, they possess the power of mindfulness and recollection;
third, they are capable of diligence. For these reasons, all Buddhas appear only in the Southern Continent.

The western continent, Aparagoyānī, is called *Goyānī* in Sanskrit and translated into Chinese as "Ox-Trade" (*Niuhuo*). This is because there are many oxen there, and they use oxen as their currency;
thus it is named "Ox-Trade. It lies to the west of Mount Sumeru. Its land is shaped like a full moon, measuring eight thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
The faces of its inhabitants are also like the full moon, and the human body is sixty cubits tall. Their lifespan is five... [years].

The lifespan is one hundred years, yet there are those who die prematurely. On this continent, people are capable of giving rise to the afflictions of views and thoughts and of committing the three grades of evil.

Although they do not see a Buddha, there are Arhats who go there to preach the Dharma and provide instruction; thus, they are able to practice the supramundane virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, meditation, and wisdom.
The northern continent of Uttarakuru (Sanskrit: *Uttara-kuru*) is translated as "Superior Place" (*shengchu*) or "High and Exalted.
Compared to the other three continents, its ground is the highest and most exalted because its merit is the most superior. It lies to the north of Mount Sumeru;
its land is square, resembling a pond, measuring ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. The faces of its inhabitants also resemble the shape of the land, and so do their bodies.
They are thirty-two cubits tall. The human lifespan is one thousand years, and no one dies prematurely. They do not grasp at "mine," nor do they commit the ten unwholesome deeds;
upon the end of their lives, they will certainly be reborn in the heavens. There, they experience only pure bliss without suffering, and they have no fear of impermanence.
Because they cannot be transformed by the Buddha-dharma, they constitute one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
*Hé* (轄) is pronounced with a level tone (*xián*); it refers to the iron linchpin at the head of a chariot axle. The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "The Director of Chariots greased the linchpins."
The axle sound follows. That which holds the wheel of the chariot is the hub (*nābhi*).
The "nine grades from lowest-lowest" refer to the afflictions of thought (*vitarka*) within the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms;
each stage is divided into nine grades, totaling eighty-one grades. The "lowest-lowest of the nine grades" refers specifically to the final ninth grade.
Having exhausted the ninth grade of the lowest-of-the-low defilements, one never again regresses;
thus, one accords with the single *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is both conditioned and unconditioned, meaning that the afflictions of view and thought have already been severed.
When the remaining manifest physical body has not yet been extinguished, this is called *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
Second is *nirvāṇa without remainder*, which means that both the two delusions—viewing and affliction—and the five aggregates of the received body are simultaneously extinguished without any residue;
this is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*.
The second fascicle:
*zhǐ* (pronounced as in *zhǐyīn*) means a whetstone. "The royal roads were like whetstones" praises the virtue of King Wen of Zhou; it means they were as level and fair as a whetstone.
Thus it says "there was the Way. That the whetstone is straight refers to the fact that the Way is level and straight.
*Lei* (pronounced like *lei*) means emaciated or thin.

Among the five dull proclivities (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the first is the proclivity of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*). "Desire" (*rāga*) refers to the act of grasping and taking that knows no satiety.

This means that sentient beings are greedily attached to the worldly forms, desires, wealth, and treasures; they indulge their minds and emotions without ever reaching satisfaction. It is because of this craving...
Driven and enslaved by delusion, one transmigrates through the three realms.

Second is the latent tendency of anger (*pratighānuśaya*). Anger is fury; it refers to the arising of various forms of anger toward sentient beings who present disagreeable objects, thereby causing affliction and turmoil for oneself and others.
Driven and enslaved by this delusion of anger, one transmigrates through the three realms.
The third is the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*). Ignorance is precisely delusion and lack of clarity; it is folly.
This means that all sentient beings, with minds clouded by delusion, take objects as their conditions and are unable to clearly comprehend all phenomena.
Driven and enslaved by this folly, they transmigrate through the three realms.
The four latent tendencies of pride (*māna-anuśaya*): Pride consists of relying on oneself and disparaging others.

This refers to sentient beings who, relying on their own lineage, wealth, nobility, virtue, or talent, look down upon others. Driven and enslaved by this conceited mind, they transmigrate through the three realms.
The fifth is the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*). Doubt is indecision and lack of resolution.

It refers to sentient beings whose deluded minds deviate from principle and who are unable to penetrate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Because they are driven and enslaved by this doubt, they transmigrate through the three realms;
therefore, it is called a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
The five views of gain (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) include the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). As for the view of a self-identity:

it refers to sentient beings falsely conceptualizing as a "self" within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
Driven by this view of a self-identity, the mind and spirit are coerced into wandering through saṃsāra without ceasing.

The second is the latent tendency of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Regarding "extreme views": this refers to sentient beings who, with respect to their prior bodies, either cling to them as being annihilated or cling to them as being eternal;
thus they each grasp at one extreme. Driven by these extreme views, they enslave the mind and spirit.
They flow and revolve without ceasing.

Regarding the three latent tendencies of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*): "false view" refers to sentient beings grasping at principles with a distorted mind, repudiating cause and effect, and severing all roots of goodness.
Driven by this false view, they enslave their mental faculties, causing them to flow and revolve without end.
*Xi* (to cease) means to sever.
Regarding the four *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-anuśaya* (proclivities of clinging to views): *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* refers to sentient beings who, among various views, adhere to one particular view;
within that which is not the truly supreme Dharma, they erroneously calculate it to be *nirvāṇa*, giving rise to a mind of grasping and attachment toward false views.
...in the midst [of these views], one clings to them as being right view. Driven by this clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the mind and spirit are driven about, wandering without cessation.

Regarding the five types of clinging, first is clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This refers to various non-Buddhists who, regarding what is not true morality, erroneously take it to be morality.
Its function is to serve as the basis for fruitless exertion and suffering, such as the false precepts of cows, dogs, chickens, and so forth, as well as [the practice of] throwing oneself into fire.
Tearing out one's hair, scorching the body with the five fires, and abstaining from food and drink—regarding these as true precepts and adopting them for practice;

even if one has received the Buddha’s precepts, yet aims to be reborn in heaven or to become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and the like—all such cases are subsumed under the "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Because one is driven and enslaved by this clinging to precepts, the spirit must inevitably transmigrate without ceasing; therefore, it is called a "proclivity" (*anuśaya*). It is associated with both [wholesome and unwholesome states].
The questioner asks: Why are the two views—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—absent from the [remaining] three truths?

The answer is: The two views of self-identity and extremes exist only with respect to the fruit of suffering. To grasp the body as a self is called the view of a self-identity; to grasp the body as being subject to annihilation or permanence is called the view of extremes.

Since the other three truths are not the "body," these two views do not occur there. The questioner asks: For what reason does one who clings to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) become deluded regarding the path to the cessation of suffering?

[Question: Are these two truths? [Answer: The essence of the precepts is suffering; yet one grasps them as purity, and thus they are described as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Wrong precepts are not the Path;

yet one grasps them as the Path, and thus one is deluded regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). [Question: Why is there no grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) within the origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), or the path (*mārga*) [truths]?

[Answer: There are two types of grasping at precepts: first, reckoning what is not a cause to be a cause, which arises from being deluded regarding the fruit of suffering; second, reckoning what is not the Path to be the Path, which arises from being deluded regarding the Path.

Because the Path arises, the Accumulation (samudaya) ceases and is non-existent. Regarding the cessation of the Accumulation as being free from the three views: the two views of self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and the attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) are the root of suffering.

At the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi) is already abandoned; because it relies upon the body, it is also abandoned along with the Truth of Accumulation.
Furthermore, one does not conceive of the Path or Non-path as being the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya). Moreover, because these are not stages of cultivation, they are all [abandoned].
There is no clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*) that can be severed.
"Du" (獨) refers to sound; it means solitary or alone. One who is old and without children is called "du. Because one has neither husband nor children, one is said to be "single and alone" (*dudan*).
The character *sì* (伺) has four meanings: to wait for, to observe, and to investigate—that is, to keep watch and conduct inquiries.

Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If, throughout all worlds, among the sentient beings of the six realms of existence, there were not even a speck of dust that could escape lust, it would be the root of birth and death;
conversely, if one turns away from it, [birth and death] will not continue. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "All..."
All sentient beings, because of lustful desire, take up their proper life and nature; one should know that saṃsāra has craving as its root.
Since various desires assist in the arousal of this craving-nature, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.

Even if one possesses meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), so long as one does not sever lust—even if it be the Māras or Māra-daughters—one will not sever lust while practicing meditative concentration; such "Māra-concentration" accords with delusion and is easily achieved.

Those whose merit is profound constitute the superior grade; those whose merit is shallow constitute the middle and lower grades. Although they have not severed desire, they cultivate meditative concentration and merit;
according to the excellence or inferiority of their merit, they thus form three grades. By means of the power of false concentration, they obtain the five supernormal powers as a karmic retribution;

by means of tainted merit, they are born into the realm of celestial demons (*deva*). Having attained a small degree of concentration, they fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, each claiming for themselves—
Having attained the Unsurpassed Way, one might commit the four grave offenses and fall into hell; yet now, by the merit of practicing dhyāna, one merely falls into the paths of demons and ghosts.
If one considers future transmigration, one ought to experience all three miserable realms in full.
*Yuan* (垣) is pronounced *yuan*. It refers to a wall. A low wall is called a *yuan*;
a high wall is called a *yong*. *Zhe* (柵) is pronounced *zhe*. It is made by weaving wood together; it is also pronounced *shan*, meaning a fence.
The pronunciation of *bàn* (絆) is *bàn*. That which binds the feet is called *bàn*; that which binds the head is called *jī* (覊).
For *chǒu* (杻) and *xiè* (械), the upper character is pronounced *chǒu* and refers to hand-shackles; the lower character is pronounced *jiè* and is the general term for instruments of restraint.
*Luóluó* (the second character is pronounced with the departing tone): to patrol; to obstruct.
*Dān* (the first character is pronounced with the level tone). *Lán* (the final character has the phonetic value of *lán*).
*Qúyù*: the upper character is pronounced *qú*, the lower is pronounced *yù*. This refers to the mynah bird (*bāgē*).
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao of Lu, a mynah came and nested in a courtyard. A child removed the tip of its tongue and taught it to speak; it became exceedingly clever.
*Yi* (杙): pronounced as *yi*, it means a wooden peg or a stake. *Ku* (刳):
pronounced as *ku*, it means to hollow out or split open.
*Hu* (瓠): pronounced as *hu*.
The *krokodila* (鰐) is pronounced "E" (諤);

the *śiśumāra* (鼉) is pronounced "Da" (陀). These are species of aquatic creatures. This fish has feet and is over ten feet long; its shell is like armor, and its hide is so hard and thick that it can be used to cover drums.
"Rui" (叡) means "wisdom" (音, yīn). It signifies profound clarity and thorough penetration.
"Su" (窣) is pronounced with a departing tone;
"xī" (孫) is pronounced with a rising tone. "Qiān" (徙) means "to move" or "to transfer. "Yí" (移) also means "to shift."
The pronunciation of *mǐ* (弭) is like that of *mǐ* (米). The pronunciation of *shuì* (稅) is the departing tone; "to bestow something upon another" is called *shuì*.
The pronunciation of *jiǎn* (儉) is the entering tone; it means "few" or "a year of famine."

Regarding the precept against stealing, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If the sentient beings of the six realms across all worlds do not steal in their hearts—even to the point that throughout the continuity of birth and death they take what is not given—the mere arising of such a thought constitutes an offense. Therefore, it says, 'their hearts do not steal.'"

If meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do not manifest before one, even if greed and theft are eliminated, and although one may refrain from sexual misconduct and killing, one will still fall into heterodox paths.

Spirits, goblins, and various heterodox persons are all capable of deluding and confusing such people, causing the masses to flock to them and providing them with food and clothing without stint until their very lives are exhausted.
If one does not cultivate meditative concentration, one will go directly to hell; for how could spirits, goblins, and the like ever transcend the realm of worldly toil?
Furthermore, [wealth] belongs to five families: first, water; second, fire; third, thieves; fourth, wicked children; and fifth, the government.
In the third fascicle, "yu" (瘀) is pronounced "yù"; it refers to the disease of blood congestion.
*Ān* (pronounced *yǎn*) means dark blue-black.
*Mín* (pronounced *mǐn*) means extinction; it means exhaustion.
Among the three kinds of color, one is visible and resistant form (*sanidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*). Regarding "visible and resistant form," this refers to all [such forms].
This refers to the object-field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*). It means that the forms of the world are visible to the eye, because they possess resistance (*sapratigha*) toward the eye.

Second, invisible and resistant form (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*): invisible and resistant form refers to the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) and four of the object-fields (*catvāra āyatanāni*).

This means that while the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is invisible, it is capable of confronting form; while the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) is invisible, it is capable of [confronting sound].

The auditory consciousness cannot be seen, yet it can encounter sound; the olfactory consciousness cannot be seen, yet it can encounter fragrance; the gustatory consciousness cannot be seen, yet it can encounter flavor;
the tactile consciousness cannot be seen, yet it can encounter tangibles—all of these are called the ultimate faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*).
The third is invisible and non-resistant form (*anidarśana-apratigha-rūpa*). Regarding "invisible and non-resistant form," this refers to unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
That is to say, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its object a realm previously perceived, it is termed "fallen away" (*pralīna*).
Although the five sense objects are clearly distinguished by the mental consciousness, they are all invisible and lack manifest resistance; therefore, they are classified as such.
*Shè* (pronounced *shì*) means the movement of venomous insects.
*Xiàn* (both with the departing tone) means to fall or drop.
*Zào* (with the entering tone) means to bore a hole.
*Héng* (桁): A wooden frame; it refers to a restraint. Both the restraints that bind the feet and those for the neck are called *héng*.
*Jiàng* (弶): Pronounced with a departing tone (*qiáng*). It refers to setting a snare on a path to trap birds and beasts.
"摾" (dǎng) is the same as "弶" (qiáng).
"撥般" (bōbān) is pronounced with a departing tone; it means "to emit.
"Nāga" in Sanskrit is translated here as "dragon"; the intended meaning is "dragon-reproach. The Sūtra says: "There are four causes and conditions. First..."
First, they give much in alms; second, they are full of anger; third, they wound others with contempt; fourth, they are self-exalting. The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā Sūtra* states:
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying, "Since the beginning of the kalpa, I have dwelt in the great ocean since the time of Krakucchanda Buddha."
"At that time, those with wives and children in the great ocean were very few; now, the retinue of the Dragon King is vast and numerous. The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"Those who have gone forth in the Buddha-dharma but violate the precepts and do not renounce their broken discipline are mostly reborn among the dragons.
Even if they do not fall directly into hell, there were ninety-eight billion Buddhas such as Krakucchanda and Kanakamuni."
The Muni Buddha had eight billion; the Kāśyapa Buddha had six billion;

and in my own world, there have been nine hundred and ninety billion who have already been born. For this reason, within the great ocean, their wives, children, and retinues are beyond all calculation.
Asura is translated in the Qin language as "those who do not drink wine. They possess great power and constantly engage in battle with the devas.
The old translation was "the Ugly" (wěnduāng), meaning that while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful. The new translation is "Non-deva" (fēitiān).
The retribution of these beings is most excellent, ranking immediately below the various devas; they are also called Asura. *Sura* means "deva," and because they are not devas, they are so named.
Asura. Furthermore, "sura" means upright and handsome; because they are not upright and handsome, they are called asura.
The old translation "asura" (阿修羅) and "asuluo" (阿須論) are both erroneous.
The Gandharva is here translated as "Fragrance-Body" (xiāngyīn). It is also called the "Spirit Who Transcends the Void. They do not consume wine or meat;

they sustain their bodies solely through fragrance and serve as the musicians of the Heavenly Emperor. In their previous lives, they also possessed a slight degree of anger, yet they were always fond of practicing generosity;
thus, they have now become these deities.

*Yakṣa* is translated here as "valiant" (*yǒngjiàn*) or "fierce and evil" (*bàoè*). Kumārajīva said: "In the language of Qin, it means 'noble person' (*guìrén*), or also 'light and agile' (*qīngjiàn*).
There are three kinds: first, those who walk upon the earth; second, those who move through the void; and third, celestial *yakṣas*.

They are also generally prone to anger and cruelty, fond of wine and meat, yet they practice giving. Those who fall [into this state] become earth-walking *yakṣas*. If a person is stubborn and headstrong..."
During the Liang dynasty, he practiced giving by providing carriages and horses as substitutes for his own feet; thus, he was reborn as an *ākāśa-gāmin* yakṣa.
If a person possesses a jealous mind and loves contention, yet is able to give excellent dwellings, bedding, clothing, food, and drink, they will therefore be born as a *vihāyasagāmin* yakṣa.
"Middle" (*zhong*) in meaning is translated as "swift-moving" (*jixing*); their movement is so rapid that in a single thought-moment they can travel hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*. There are...
Its light is swift; like a flowing thing in the world, people call it a falling star. Smoke issues from its mouth;
people of the world call it a broom-star (zhūxīng).
*Qiè* (pronounced jì): A clay brick; an unbaked earthenware tile or mold.

Regarding the precept against killing, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms across all worlds, even down to those as minute as a speck of dust, they cannot escape [this cycle].
They kill one another and settle their debts through retaliation; they form enmities and pass on calamities to one another. If one were to stop this, the cycle would no longer continue."

Those who practice dhyāna while harboring a murderous intent receive retribution as spirits of the divine realm; if their merit is profound and their blessings abundant, they become powerful ghosts, such as those enshrined in the sacrifices of the Five Peaks and Four Rivers.

If their merit is shallow and their blessings inferior, they are ranked among the middle or lower classes, falling under the jurisdiction of the Eight Divisions of Spirits or belonging to the classes of rākṣasas along the shores of the great ocean.
Because they have practiced meditative concentration, they all possess karmic supernormal powers that are swift and unimpeded.
Because they do not cease killing, they undergo this realm of hungry ghosts and are driven into service by the devas.

If one does not cultivate dhyāna nor cultivate merit, but practices only slaughter, one enters directly into hell without such gradations of retribution. Ghosts and spirits kill much, yet they cannot escape the wheel of suffering.
To kill living beings and eat their flesh is to be an enemy to sentient beings; how can one fail to sever this [killing] and attain the path to Bodhi? There is no [other way].
There is such a place: the Five Peaks (*pañca-giri*) are the progenitors of all mountains, lofty and venerable.
Mount Huo is the Heavenly Pillar (*dyaus-stambha*). Mount Shan is Mount Heng; Mount Heng is the Southern Peak (*dakṣiṇa-parvata*). The Eastern Peak, Mount Tai, is in Jiuzhou.
The Western Peak, Mount Hua, is in Hongnong—present-day Shanzhou, Henan Prefecture, Henan Province. It is also known by the alternative name Hongnong.
The Northern Peak, Mount Heng, is located within Dingzhou. The [Central] Peak, Mount Song, is located within Yingzhou. Regarding the Four Great Rivers:
the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji are the four great rivers. The Yangtze River originates from Mount Min. The Yellow River originates from Mount Jishi;
coming from the position of Qian (the northwest), it flows with one bend every thousand li, completing nine bends before entering the sea. The Huai River originates from Ruoning in Henan.
It flows through Xinyang County of the Prefecture, then enters the sea at Andong County of Huai'an Prefecture in Zhili.
The Ji River originates from Mount Min (the "Min" sound is pronounced *min*). Mount Min is located one *li* south of Yiluo in Minzhou, extending in a continuous range.
In the region of Shu, an area of two thousand li, all is called Mount Min.
*Prajñā* (discerning wisdom) is termed the fourfold unimpeded knowledge (*catur-pratisaṃvid*); it refers to the Bodhisattva’s clear and lucid wisdom regarding these four dharmas.

Because they penetrate all things without obstruction, they are called the four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). Because their eloquent exposition is harmonious and pervasive, they are also called the four unhindered analytical powers (*catasro nirukti-pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

First is the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): this refers to the Bodhisattva’s thorough understanding and penetration of the principles and meanings of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Because it is unimpeded, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Second is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): this refers to the Bodhisattva’s thorough penetration of the names of all phenomena, distinguishing them without impediment;
therefore, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.

Third is the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). This refers to the Bodhisattva’s ability to expound the names, meanings, and principles of all phenomena in accordance with the diverse languages and dialects of all sentient beings, enabling each individual to achieve understanding.
Because his eloquent exposition is unimpeded, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of expression.

The fourth is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). This refers to the Bodhisattva’s ability to preach the Dharma in accordance with the inclinations and capacities of all sentient beings.
Because it is perfectly integrated and free from obstruction, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence.
*Li* (勵) is pronounced like *li* (例). It means to exert effort. "Human aggregates" (*rén yīn*):
