When consuming edible food, one contemplates it as impure, like eating the flesh of one's own child. Regarding contact, volition, and consciousness nutriments, one maintains the perception of their disintegration.
Thus, the practitioner who reflects and recollects in this manner, based on detachment from desire and defilement—this is [the perception of impurity].

This is called the perception of the impurity of food. Having approached it and practiced it extensively, one gives rise to clarity, attains clarity, and acquires the factors of clarity, thereby enabling clarity to become vast.
This is called the factor conducive to enlightenment consisting of the perception of the impurity of food.
The five factors conducive to enlightenment consisting of the perception of non-delight in all worlds:

that is, the sense of wearying detachment and lack of delight toward all worlds—the world of hell-beings, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, the world of gods, and the world of sentient beings.

One feels weary of and does not delight in it; one abandons, detaches from, and does not accept it. Just as with worldly practitioners, whatever perceptions or recollections there may be—these are called the perception of non-delight in all the world.
Having approached, cultivated, and practiced this extensively, one gives rise to clear knowledge, attains clear knowledge, and gains the factors conducive to clear knowledge.
That which enables one to make clarity vast is called the "factor of clarity consisting of the perception of the unattractiveness of all the world.
Sixth, the factor of clarity consisting of the perception of death: either beneath a tree or in the open air, one reflects thus:
"I am subject to the nature of death; there is the peril of death. Other sentient beings as well are subject to the nature of death; they too have the peril of death. If on the ground...

Whether they dwell in hell, as animals, hungry ghosts, devas, or humans, all sentient beings who come and go within the cycle of birth and death and are designated as "sentient beings" possess the nature of death and the calamities of death.

Contemplating in this way the relinquishing of the body through the aggregates, one recollects death, contemplates death, knows death, understands death, and awakens to death. If a practitioner thus forms or recollects such thoughts, this is...

This is called the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*). Having approached it and practiced it extensively, one gives rise to knowledge, attains knowledge, and acquires the factors conducive to knowledge, thereby enabling knowledge to become vast.
This is what is meant by the "factors conducive to knowledge regarding the perception of death" (*maraṇasaṃjñā-vidyābhāgīya-dharma*).

What are the six factors that cause delight? As with a bhikkhu who, having become delighted, gives rise to joy; having become joyful, his body becomes tranquil; having become tranquil in body, he experiences happiness;
having experienced happiness, his mind becomes concentrated; and having attained concentration of mind, he knows and sees things as they truly are.
These are called the six factors that cause delight.

What are the six factors of right awakening that are without rapture, from mindfulness of right awakening up to equanimity of right awakening? These are called the six factors of right awakening without rapture.
As for the "sevenfold path," it refers to the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*). "Awakening" means clear comprehension; that is, the clear comprehension of what has been cultivated.
The Dharma is either authentic or spurious. "Factors" (*aṅga*) refers to constituent parts;

that is to say, these seven types of factors each have their own distinct branches and boundaries, and because they do not intermingle or become confused, they are called the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), also known as the Seven Limbs of Enlightenment. Among them, the three factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*) belong to wisdom (*prajñā*);

the three factors of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and concentration (*samādhi*) belong to meditative absorption (*samādhi*); and the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) belongs to both.
Wisdom. Thus, the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "By practicing these seven factors of enlightenment, one immediately enters the Path.

First, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). "Investigation" (*vicaya*) means discernment. This refers to when one employs wisdom to observe all phenomena;
it is the ability to skillfully distinguish between the true and the false, so as not to erroneously grasp at deceptive dharmas. Therefore, it is called the investigation of phenomena.
The Factors of Enlightenment (bodhipakṣa). Second, the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*). "Purity" (*vi*) means being unmixed; "progression" (*pra*) means being uninterrupted.

This refers to when one cultivates the various factors of the path, being well able to discern clearly, not engaging in useless ascetic practices, and always [abiding] within the truly authentic Dharma.
Being able to apply the mind with single-minded concentration and without interruption is therefore called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Third, the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): joy is gladness; it refers to the time when the mind realizes the true Dharma and attains gladness.

One is well able to awaken to this. This joy does not arise from inverted phenomena; because one abides in the true joy of the Dharma, it is called the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Fourth, the factor of awakening of relinquishment (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): "relinquishment" means to abandon and eliminate. That is to say, at the time of abandoning and eliminating all views and afflictions, one is well...

One is able to awaken to and comprehend [reality], thereby eliminating false and deceptive phenomena and increasing genuine roots of goodness; thus, it is called the awakening factor of investigation (*pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Fifth, the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): "Equanimity" means relinquishment, specifically the relinquishing of objects of attachment as perceived through views. It is wholesome...
One is able to clearly discern that which is false and unreal, never again recollecting it; therefore, it is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): Concentration refers to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). This means that when one gives rise to meditative absorption, one is well able to discern all dhyānas so that afflictions and deluded thoughts do not arise; this is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
The Seven Factors of Enlightenment: *Smṛti* (mindfulness) refers to recollection.
This means that when practicing the various factors of the path, one is able to discern them well and constantly maintains the balance between concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

If the mind becomes dull or drowsy, one should practice the three factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*), observing all dharmas so as not to fall into dullness. If the mind becomes agitated or restless—

One should employ the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to eliminate faults of body and speech; employ the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to relinquish discursive wisdom;

and employ the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to enter right meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), gathering the distracted mind so that it does not become agitated. This is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
What are the seven perceptions? First is the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
By drawing near to it and practicing it extensively, having practiced it extensively, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless (*amṛta*). For what reason is this said?
When one recognizes through the mind that the perception of impurity causes the lustful mind to retreat, subside, and fail to expand, it should be gradually eliminated until it is exhausted.
Having turned away from it, having become disenchanted with it, and having attained right abiding— just as a sinew, a bird’s feather, or a *tṛṇa* grass stalk, when thrown into a fire,
shrivels and curls up without expanding and subsequently is consumed— having thus turned away, become disenchanted, and attained right abiding, this is called [the perception of impurity].
The perception of purity.
Second, the perception of the impurity of food. One should draw near to it and practice it extensively.

Having practiced it extensively, one attains great fruit and reward, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless nectar (*amṛta*). With a mind that knows and discriminates the perception of the impurity of food, regarding morsels of food...

The mind that feeds upon it recedes and does not advance; it shall gradually be eliminated until it is exhausted. Having turned away from it, having become weary of it and detached from it, one dwells correctly.
This is called the perception of the impurity of food.
Third, the perception of the lack of delight in all the world: by drawing near to it and practicing it extensively, and having practiced it extensively, one attains [it].
Great is the fruit of retribution; one attains great merit and reaches the deathless (*amṛta*). For what reason is this said?

It is because the mind knows and discerns all worldly perceptions of dissatisfaction; the mind’s various worldly perceptions recede and do not advance, gradually being eliminated until they are exhausted.
Having turned away from them, having become weary of and detached from them, one dwells correctly, like a sinew, like a bird’s feather, like...
Just as *tūla* grass, when thrown into a fire, curls up and shrivels without unfurling, and is subsequently consumed and exhausted;

so too, one should mentally discern the perception of the lack of delight in all the world. This causes various perceptions of the world to recede and not advance, gradually leading to their total elimination.
Having turned away from them, become disenchanted with them, and attained detachment, one dwells correctly in this state. This is called the perception of the lack of delight in all the world.
The perception of pleasure.
The four perceptions of death: by approaching, frequently practicing, and training extensively in them, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the Deathless.
For what reason is this said? Because the mind knows and discerns the perception of death.
Relying upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), one becomes conceited; with the life-faculty fixed, the mind remains complacent and constantly attached to it.
When such [attachment] is completely severed without remainder, this is called the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*).
Regarding the five perceptions of impermanence: by drawing near to them and practicing them extensively, one attains great fruit and reward upon such extensive practice;
one attains great merit and reaches the deathless (*amṛta*). For what reason is this said?
When the mind knows and discerns the perception of impermanence, its inclination toward gain, fame, and honor recedes and does not advance, until it is gradually eliminated and exhausted.

Having turned away and become weary through detachment, one abides correctly. Like a sinew, like a bird’s feather, or like *tūla* grass thrown into a fire—which shrivels and curls up without unfolding and is subsequently consumed—so too does the mind, through the discernment of the perception of impermanence, withdraw from gain, fame, and honor;
the mind retreats and does not advance, gradually being eliminated until it is utterly exhausted, having turned away and become weary through detachment.
Having thus correctly established oneself, this is called the perception of impermanence.
Sixth, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent: by drawing near to it and practicing it extensively, and having practiced it extensively, one attains a great fruit and reward.
One attains great merit and reaches the deathless nectar (amṛta). For what reason is this said?
It is because one’s mind knows and discerns the perceptions of impermanence and suffering regarding indolence, laziness, lack of faith, negligence, lack of diligence, and lack of contemplation.
They give rise to terror; they are intensely pressed by great fear, as if facing death. Raising one’s strength, one contemplates the perception of impermanence;
this is called the perception of impermanence as suffering.
Seventh is the perception of non-self in suffering. By drawing near to it and practicing it extensively, and having practiced it extensively, one attains a great fruit and reward.
One attains great merit and great ambrosia. For what reason is this said?
It is because such a mind discriminates suffering and the notion of non-self, yet regarding the conscious body and all external objects, it calculates them as "self" and "what belongs to self."
Giving rise to conceit and the like, one is entirely separated from tranquility and true liberation; this is called the perception of suffering as non-self.

What are the seven factors conducive to concentration? They are right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness. These are the seven factors conducive to concentration.
The Eightfold Path refers to the Eightfold Noble Path. These eight factors are called "right" because they do not proceed by way of partiality or deviation;
they are called "path" because they can lead directly to nirvana.
First, Right View: this refers to a person cultivating the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). As for the untainted path, it consists of precept, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*).
One who cultivates this path is able to sever the tainted birth and death (*sāsrava-jāti-maraṇa*) of the three realms. It means seeing the Four Noble Truths with clarity.
To destroy the various false views of outsiders, such as those concerning existence and non-existence, is right view.
Second is right thought: this refers to when a person perceives the Four Truths, they contemplate with right mindfulness, observing and deliberating.
Causing contemplation to increase is right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

Third is right speech (*samyag-vāc*): when a person, by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), constantly restrains their verbal karma and remains far removed from all false and unreal speech, this is called right speech.
The Four Right Actions (*samyak-karmānta*): This refers to a person using untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to cultivate and collect the mind, abiding in pure right action.
Regarding "pure right action": it refers to supramundane wholesome actions such as morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
To sever all erroneous and delusive conduct is what constitutes right action.
The five right modes of livelihood: this means that those who have left the household life should distance themselves from the five kinds of wrong livelihood for the sake of gain and support.
They should always sustain their lives by begging for alms; this is called right livelihood.
Sixth, Right Diligence (*samyag-vīrya*): "Pure" means unmixed; "progressive" means uninterrupted.

This refers to when a person diligently cultivates the path of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), with single-minded devotion and without interruption. This is called right diligence.

Seventh is Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*): this refers to a person’s recollection of the right path of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the five methods for settling the mind that assist the path;
being capable of advancing toward Nirvana, this is called Right Mindfulness.

Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): This refers to a person gathering all scattered thoughts so that body and mind are tranquil, correctly abiding in the principle of true emptiness, and remaining resolutely immovable; this is called right concentration.
The "eight liberations" (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*): "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) means to turn away from; "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) means to cast off. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"One turns one's back on these five pure desires and abandons this mind of attachment; therefore, they are called 'liberations.

By practicing these contemplations, one gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), exhausts all afflictions of view and thought within the three realms, realizes the fruit of Arhatship, and is then renamed as the 'eight deliverances' (*aṣṭau vimuktayaḥ*)."

Regarding "pure and clean five desires": if they are the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are called coarse and base five desires, and are termed impure.
If they are the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are called pure and clean five desires.
Regarding "untainted wisdom" (*anāsravajñāna*): this refers to the wisdom by which those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and others sever [afflictions].

It eliminates delusion and karma, so that one does not fall back into the cycle of birth and death. The "three realms" refer to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. Regarding "delusions of views and thoughts":
when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmas*), it gives rise to various discriminations; these are called "delusions of views.

When the five faculties, such as the eye, encounter the five sense objects, such as visible forms, they give rise to various cravings and attachments; these are called "delusions of thought. In Sanskrit, this is *Arhat*.
Han: *Huá-yán* (Chinese) translates as "Aśaikṣa" (One Beyond Training).

First: possessing internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms. This means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as decaying, impure, and not to be desired for its loveliness;
with a mind settled in meditative concentration, they further imagine the skin and flesh falling away.
One merely sees white bones emitting light of eight colors. Regarding these eight-colored lights:
one sees the color of earth as a pure, yellowish-white ground; one sees the color of water as clear water within a deep pool;
one sees the color of fire as a pure fire from clean fuel and incense smoke; one sees the color of wind as a dustless, clear breeze; and one sees the color blue as gold.
One sees a brilliant mountain; it appears yellow like a *campaka* flower, red like the dawn clouds of spring, and white like jade or snow.
Therefore, it is said that there are internal forms. Furthermore, because the craving of the desire realm is difficult to sever, [one contemplates these forms].

Although one has already observed the impurity of internal form for oneself, it is nevertheless necessary to further observe the forms of others through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) in order to engender revulsion and seek its cessation.

Furthermore, it is said that one "observes external forms"; this refers to the stage of the first *vairāgya* (detachment), which occurs within the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the First Dhyāna Heaven.

Second, "internally perceiving no form while externally perceiving forms": This means that once the practitioner has entered the second dhyāna, they have extinguished the perception of form within their own body;

hence it is said, "internally perceiving no form. Furthermore, because the craving for desire-realm objects is difficult to sever, they continue to contemplate the signs of external impurity to engender revulsion, seeking thereby to eliminate it; hence it is further called "externally perceiving."
Form. This is the second stage of liberation (*vimokṣa*). It occurs within the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the Second Dhyāna Heaven.
Third, one realizes with the body the pure liberation; "pure" here refers to taking a pure aspect as the object.
That is to say, after the practitioner has completed the second liberation, they discard the impure aspects of external forms and instead refine [the mind] within meditative concentration.
One practices the eightfold radiance of light, which is pure, brilliant, and like the color of exquisite jewels; hence it is called the "pure liberation" (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
As the mind becomes luminous and pure, bliss gradually increases and pervades the entire body, resulting in total serenity; therefore, it is further called "bodily realization.
This constitutes the third stage of liberation (*vimokṣa*), situated within the meditative concentration of the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
The fourth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*).

This means that after the practitioner has, following the first liberation, discarded the impure physical form of their own body; and after the second liberation, has further discarded the color of the white bones within the body;
and after [the third], has further discarded all impure colors of external bodies—there remains only the eight kinds of pure forms.
Form all abides in dependence upon the mind; if the mind relinquishes form, form immediately perishes and ceases.

When the single mind takes emptiness as its object and accords with emptiness, one enters the meditative absorption of the base of infinite space. Therefore, it is called the "rejection of the base of space.
This is the fourth stage of rejection, situated within the meditative absorptions of the Four Dhyāna Heavens.

The Deliverance (vimokṣa) of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*): This refers to when a practitioner, having relinquished the Sphere of Infinite Space, enters meditative absorption with the mind focused single-mindedly on consciousness.
At that time, they contemplate that this concentration, as well as its basis—the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth—is entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Regarding "impermanent": it means that the body of the five aggregates ultimately ends in destruction. Regarding "suffering": it means that the body is subject to birth.

It refers to the suffering of being oppressed by death and so forth. "Empty" means that the body is originally empty, having been formed through the provisional combination of the four great elements.
"Selfless" means that since the four great elements are each separate, who is the self? It is deceptive and unreal.
The mind gives rise to revulsion and turns away from it, rather than accepting or clinging to it; therefore, it is called the "liberation through turning away from the sphere of consciousness.

Sixth, the liberation through turning away from the sphere of nothingness: This refers to when a practitioner, having relinquished the sphere of consciousness, focuses the mind single-mindedly on the sphere of nothingness and enters meditative absorption.
At that time, they contemplate this concentration as being entirely impermanent and suffering, based upon the five aggregates and so forth.

It is empty and selfless, deceptive and unreal; one gives rise to revulsion toward it and does not accept or cling to it. Therefore, it is called the "rejection of the sphere of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vairāgya*).

Seventh, the rejection of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vairāgya*): This refers to when the practitioner, having relinquished the sphere of nothingness...

Regarding the stage: when one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with a single-minded focus, one contemplates this very absorption—in terms of the five aggregates and so forth—as entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as deceptive and unreal. Thus, a sense of revulsion arises in the mind, and one does not harbor attachment;
therefore, it is called the "rejection of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

The eighth is the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-vimokṣa*). "Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to experiencing; "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to conceptualization.

These are the two mental factors of feeling and perception among the five aggregates. It means that because the practitioner is weary of these minds being distracted and wishes to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for rest, they turn away from and cease the various minds of feeling and perception. This is called the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception.

The Eight Bases of Mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*). Regarding the Eight Bases of Mastery: after having cultivated the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), one’s contemplation becomes refined and one attains mastery over transformation.
Whether [the object] is pure or impure, one can master it at will. The *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The first two bases of mastery are situated in the first dhyāna; the third and fourth bases of mastery are situated in the second dhyāna; the fifth..."
Up to the eighth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), its locus is in the fourth dhyāna. As for why the bases of mastery are not established in the third dhyāna:
it is because the bliss of the third dhyāna heavens is so abundant that the mind is purely [absorbed] therein; therefore, they are not established there.
First, internally perceiving the form of a body, one externally perceives forms that are small, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
This means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as putrid, impure, and not to be desired.
With a mind settled in meditative concentration, they further imagine the skin and flesh falling away, seeing only eight-colored rays of light. Therefore...
It is said that there are internal forms; furthermore, because the path of contemplation has not yet increased, if one were to contemplate many forms, it would be difficult to maintain concentration.
Therefore, one contemplates few forms. For this reason, one contemplates the impurity of one's own body and also contemplates that the bodies of those one loves are likewise impure;
thus it is said, "externally contemplating few forms, whether beautiful or ugly," which refers to contemplating all external forms.
The fruit of wholesome karma is called "beautiful"; the fruit of unwholesome karma is called "ugly.

At times, when the mind is focused on a single point and one contemplates forms within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those forms capable of giving rise to lustful desire are pure forms and are called "beautiful";
those capable of giving rise to anger and hatred are impure forms and are called "ugly. "Superior knowledge and superior vision" refers to observing the mind alone.
Matured. Regarding beautiful forms, the mind does not feel greedy attachment; regarding ugly forms, the mind does not feel aversion.
Second: having the perception of internal form, one externally perceives many forms, whether beautiful or ugly.

This is called "superior knowledge and superior vision," meaning that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance and characteristics of their own physical body as decaying, impure, and unattractive.
Joyful, with the mind settled in one-pointed concentration, one further visualizes the skin and flesh falling away, seeing only white bones emitting light of eight colors;
thus it is said, "internally possessing the perception of form. When the contemplation of the internal body is matured, then even though external forms are numerous, they pose no hindrance.
This is what is meant by: "contemplating one corpse in detail, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and a million."
Regarding the corpse: when one contemplates it as bloated, one sees all things as bloated; this remains the case even through the stages of decay, putrefaction, bluish discoloration, and flaying.
Therefore, it is said that "one externally contemplates forms" and "knows and perceives the beautiful and the ugly," as explained in the section on the first *abhibhāyatana* (base of mastery).
Third, being internally without the perception of form, one perceives externally forms that are limited, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
This means that once the practitioner has entered the second dhyāna, they have extinguished the perception of internal form; therefore, it is said to be "internally without the perception of form."

Furthermore, because the path of contemplation has not yet increased, if one were to contemplate many forms, there would be fear that they could not be maintained; therefore, one contemplates few forms.
For this reason, one contemplates the impurity of one's own body and also contemplates that the bodies of those one loves are likewise impure.
Thus it is said: "Externally contemplating few forms. The remainder is as explained previously.
Fourth, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.

This means that once the practitioner has entered the second dhyāna, they have extinguished the perception of form within their own body; therefore, it is said that there is no perception of internal forms.
When one observes that the internal physical form is non-existent, then even though external physical forms are numerous, they likewise present no obstruction.

This means that by clearly observing a single corpse, one proceeds to observe ten million corpses; when observing a single bloated corpse, one sees all bloated corpses, and the same applies to those that are putrefied, decayed, and falling apart.
Thus, one gains superior knowledge and superior discernment regarding the beautiful and the ugly.
The visualization is as before. This is because practitioners find the afflictions of the desire realm difficult to overcome;

therefore, within the second dhyāna, they again cultivate the third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) to eliminate the afflictions of the desire realm without remainder, causing the path of contemplation to progress, become firm and unshakable, and their skillful power to increase further.

The five blue spheres of mastery (*nīla-ābhibhvāyatana*): This refers to the practitioner’s contemplation of radiant blue color, which surpasses the blue signs perceived within the eightfold light of the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Because one does not give rise to craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), they are called "spheres of mastery."

The sixth, the Yellow Mastery (pīta-abhibhvāyatana): This refers to the practitioner’s contemplation of a radiant yellow color, which surpasses the perception of the yellow sign seen within the eightfold light of the Deliverances (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ).
Furthermore, because one does not give rise to craving for dharmas, it is called a "Mastery."

The seventh is the red *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery). This refers to the practitioner’s contemplation of a blazing red color, which surpasses the red appearance seen within the eight-colored radiances of the *vimokṣa* (liberations).
Furthermore, because one does not give rise to craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), it is called a sphere of mastery.
The eight white spheres of mastery (*śubha-vimokṣa-āyatana*): This refers to the practitioner contemplating white light that shines brilliantly.

Because this surpasses the white appearance seen within the eight-colored lights of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and because one does not give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), they are called "spheres of mastery."

The "ninefold path" refers to the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*). "Nine" means there are nine types in total, from the first dhyāna up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*).
"Successive" means that when a person enters these meditative absorptions, their wisdom is profound and sharp.

One is able to emerge from the first dhyāna and enter the first dhyāna once again; thus proceeding in succession, the moments of mind continue one after another without the arising of divergent thoughts, uninterrupted and unmixed.
"Samādhi" (concentration) means the gathering of the mind so that it is not distracted.

The Sequential Concentration of the First Dhyāna: This refers to a person practicing meditative concentration who, having abandoned the evil and unwholesome states of the desire realm, possesses directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion. In this state, concentration and insight are balanced. Regarding "possessing directed thought and sustained thought":

when the initial mind is directed toward the object, it is called directed thought; when the subtle mind discriminates the flavor of dhyāna, it is called sustained thought. This is precisely the characteristic of the concentration of the first dhyāna.
Regarding "joy and bliss born of seclusion": the mind of jubilation is called joy (*prīti*), and the mind of tranquility is called bliss (*sukha*).
Since the first dhyāna is free from the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm, this joy and bliss arise.
Regarding "concentration and contemplation being equal": contemplation is wisdom; this refers to the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom. His mind proceeds in successive order...
Entering. There is no interval of discursive thought.

Regarding the sequential concentration of the second dhyāna: when a person cultivates meditative concentration and enters the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna, they are single-mindedly without vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), and experience the joy and bliss born of concentration. As for "without vitarka and vicāra": having already entered the second dhyāna, [these are absent].

This means one immediately leaves behind the agitation and distraction of initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) of the first dhyāna. Regarding "joy and bliss born of concentration":
since initial and sustained application are absent, the mind is gathered in concentration, whereby joy and bliss arise; this is the characteristic of the concentration of the second dhyāna.
His mind enters sequentially, without the intervention of distracting thoughts.
The sequential meditative absorption of the third dhyāna: This refers to when a person cultivates meditative concentration and enters the third dhyāna from the second dhyāna.

Having abandoned joy, one dwells in equanimity and experiences bodily bliss; only the noble ones can describe this as "dwelling in bliss while possessing mindfulness and equanimity. Regarding "having abandoned joy and dwelling in equanimity":
this means that, having become weary of and detached from the great joy of the second dhyāna which is agitated and scattered, one collects the mind and does not accept it.
Regarding "experiencing bodily bliss": having already abandoned the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna, one experiences the bliss of the third dhyāna with the body.
Regarding "the noble ones being able to speak": this bliss is supreme, surpassing all other forms of bliss, and is not something known by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "abandoning mindfulness and dwelling in bliss": this means being able to abandon the joy and mindfulness of the second dhyāna, and thereby practicing the third dhyāna.
"Joy": its mind enters in succession, without any intervening distracting thoughts.
Regarding the successive concentration of the four dhyānas: when a person cultivates meditative absorption and enters the fourth dhyāna from the third dhyāna, they sever joy and bliss;
thus it is "neither joyful nor blissful. As for "severing joy and bliss," this means severing the joy of the second dhyāna and...
This is the bliss of the third dhyāna. "Neither joy nor pleasure" means that the mind is free from both good and evil, being tranquil and equanimous;
this is precisely the meditative characteristic of the fourth dhyāna. His mind enters these stages in succession, without any intervening discursive thoughts.

The five successive meditative absorptions of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). This refers to when a person cultivates dhyāna and enters the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), thereby extinguishing all signs of form (*rūpanimitta*). One does not attend to various distinct characteristics.

Regarding "extinguishing all signs of form," this means extinguishing all signs of form that are perceptible through the sense faculties and their objects, whether visible or resistant. Having thus attained the fourth dhyāna concentration...
Having done so, they still find the realm of form (rūpadhātu) unsatisfactory; because the substance of form acts as an obstruction, they do not attain mastery.

Thereupon, their minds seek liberation, and they cultivate the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi), extinguishing all signs of form so that the mind accords with the dharma of space.
Thus, one does not attend to various distinct characteristics; entering the sphere of infinite space, the mind enters sequentially without any intervening discursive thoughts.
The sequential meditative absorptions of the six bases of consciousness: This refers to when a person practices dhyāna.

Having already attained the absorption of the base of infinite space, the mind takes space as its object. Since space is boundless, if the mind dwells upon it excessively, it becomes distracted and can destroy the concentration.
Thereupon, one abandons space and turns the mind to take consciousness as its object. When the mind is in correspondence with the phenomenon of consciousness, it transcends all infinite space.
Regarding "transcending all the sphere of infinite space": having entered the sphere of consciousness, one then transcends the sphere of space.
One enters the sphere of infinite consciousness with the mind proceeding in successive stages, without any intervening discursive thoughts.

The seventh is the sequential meditative concentration of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). As for the "Sphere of Nothingness," it means not taking any internal or external objects as a cognitive focus. Regarding "internal and external objects":
the internal refers to the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the external refers to the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

This means that when a person cultivates meditative concentration and has already attained the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, they [transcend] the consciousness of the three periods of time... (three) *Note: The original text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* or a similar Abhidharma-style treatise.*

"Worlds" refers to the past, present, and future. They are immeasurable and boundless. When objects of perception are numerous, the mind becomes distracted, which can disrupt meditative concentration.
Therefore, one abandons the consciousness that takes those objects as its focus and turns the mind to take the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its object.
The mind enters this state in succession, without any intervening distracting thoughts.

The eighth is the successive attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). "Non-perception" means it is not the perception found in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
"Non-non-perception" means it is not the non-perception found in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). This refers to a person practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Having attained the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one deeply understands that the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*) is like folly, and the sphere of perception (*saṃjñāyatana*) is like an abscess or a wound.
"Like folly" is a metaphor for the absence of mental perception; "like an abscess or a wound" refers to being immediately aware of pain, which is a metaphor for the presence of mental perception.
One then abandons the sphere of nothingness and takes as an object of contemplation that which is neither with perception nor without perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is not a state of non-perception; rather, the mind enters it in successive stages without any intervening discursive thoughts.

The ninth is the sequential attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*). As for the "cessation of sensation and perception," it means that the mental states of sensation and perception are extinguished and do not arise again.
This refers to a person practicing meditative concentration who, from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters the cessation of sensation and perception.
When the time for concentration arrives, his mind becomes clear and sharp; he enters it in successive stages without any intervening distracting thoughts.
This is the sequential attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). If one attains this concentration, one will soon realize the fruit of Arhatship.
The nine contemplations of repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*) are as explained previously in the section on the precept against killing.

As for the tenfold path, it refers to the ten contemplations (*daśasaṃjñā*). The first three contemplations are taught for the purpose of severing the delusions regarding the truths (*satyadarśana-heya-kleśa*);

the middle four contemplations are taught for the purpose of severing the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*); and the final three contemplations are taught for those who cultivate the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). This is so.
When a person who destroys [defilements] cultivates these ten perceptions, they are able to sever the fetters of the three realms and realize the noble fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
First is the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*): the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as impermanent. This is called...
The perception of impermanence: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are of two kinds—first, sentient beings; second, the physical realm.
Both of these arise and perish moment by moment; therefore, they are impermanent.

Second, the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*): the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as suffering is called the perception of suffering.

If conditioned phenomena are impermanent, they are precisely suffering; because they are constantly oppressed and driven by the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering, they are termed "suffering."

The third is the perception of the non-existence of self (*anātman-saṃjñā*). It is called the perception of the non-existence of self because it is a perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all phenomena as being equally without self.
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely suffering, they are without self, because they lack autonomy.
Furthermore, since suffering arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), within this absence of intrinsic nature, a self cannot be found.
The Contemplation of the Impurity of the Four Kinds of Food: One contemplates all food and drink as existing solely due to impure causes and conditions.

For example, meat arises from semen, blood, and the urinary tract; likewise, one should contemplate butter, curd, and so forth according to their respective origins, seeing them all as entirely impure.

The fifth is the perception of the world as unattractive (*lokānabhirati-saṃjñā*). The perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all worlds as unattractive is called the perception of the world as unattractive.
There are two kinds of worlds: first, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); [and second, the world of the environment].
Second is the realm, which possesses faults and evils and is not to be relished.
There are six perceptions of death: the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates death is called the perception of death.
If one’s karmic retribution for a single lifetime is constantly pursued by these two kinds of death, then one cannot guarantee that the next breath will follow the outgoing breath.

The Seven Contemplations on Impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*): The contemplation that accords with the wisdom perceiving the impurity of one’s own body and those of others is called the contemplation on impurity.
If one contemplates this body, one finds within it thirty-six substances; externally, foul secretions constantly flow from the nine orifices.
From birth until death, there is not a single thing that is pure.

The Eight Contemplations of Abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃjñāḥ*): The contemplation associated with the wisdom that perceives nirvāṇa as being free from birth and death is called the contemplation of abandonment.
The practitioner reflects: "If nirvāṇa is pure and free from afflictions, I shall abandon the fetters and realize nirvāṇa."
Ninth, the perception of detachment (*viveka-saṃjñā*): the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates nirvana as being detached from saṃsāra is called the perception of detachment.
The practitioner reflects: "If nirvana is pure and detached from saṃsāra, I shall detach from saṃsāra and realize nirvana."

The Ten Perceptions of Exhaustion (*kṣaya-saṃjñā*): The perception associated with wisdom that contemplates the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as birth and death, within nirvāṇa is called the perception of exhaustion.
The practitioner reflects: "If nirvāṇa is pure, then the fetters, as well as birth and death, are eternally exhausted."
When the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the karma of birth and death are exhausted, one immediately realizes *nirvāṇa*.

The ten rectitudes (*daśa ṛjūni*) refer to right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right liberation, and right knowledge; these are called the ten rectitudes.

The ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (spheres of totality) are also called the ten *kṛtsna-samādhis*. The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "The eight *vimokṣas* (liberations) serve as the initial gateway;
the eight *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery) constitute the intermediate practice; and the spheres of totality represent the final accomplishment.

This means that when both types of contemplation are fully perfected, the essence of dhyāna finally achieves completion. These concentrations are called 'pervading all places' because they proceed from the object of contemplation."

The name is derived from the pervasiveness of the object. In the meditative absorptions where blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness pervade all places, there are four [absorptions] which refer to taking the blue color seen within the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) and the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*) and causing it to pervade all places so that everything becomes blue;
the other three absorptions are likewise. As for the latter six, it refers to [the following] therein:
One then takes up the earth-forms seen within the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) and the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*), causing them to pervade all places without exception.

The same applies to the remaining five meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Regarding the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*): with a single perception, one contemplates above, below, and across as non-dual and immeasurable.

What is meant by "earth"? It refers to the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and the earth-magnitude (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*); this is called "earth. What is meant by "one"? [It is the state of being singular.]
"Entirety" (*sarva*) means that if there are no remaining skillful means, it is called "entirety. What is meant by "one" (*eka*)?
If one is alone and not associated with other realms—just as when a person enters the earth-totality (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*)—this is "one. What is meant by "contemplating the mind"?

It is being undistracted, inseparable, and focused exclusively on the perception of the earth. What are "above, below, and across"? "Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; "across" [refers to]...
"Extensive" refers to the four directions. It is like a person who contemplates the earth both above and below, as well as lengthwise and crosswise, knowing, understanding, and experiencing it;
this is called "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise. What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"? There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality lengthwise and crosswise.
There is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability lengthwise and crosswise—this non-duality and immeasurability consist solely of the perception of earth.
Immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and without end; regarding these as being without differentiated thought—this is called the "immeasurable without duality.
The rest should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the eleven branches of the path: they are the eleven liberative entries (*vimokṣāyatana*). First: as when a bhikṣu is detached from desire.
Abandoning unwholesome and evil states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
Thus he correctly trains in and correctly generates this concentration. Once he has completely trained in and generated it, he knows it all to be impermanent and subject to cessation;
knowing and seeing it as it truly is, he cuts off all taints, and his mind attains liberation. Although [he has not yet...]
Having severed all outflows (*āsrava*), through the desire for the Dharma and the joy of the Dharma, they sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāḥ*).
Being born there by transformation (*upapāduka*), they attain parinirvāṇa and do not return to this world; this is called the first liberation.

Second: Just as a bhikṣu, having stilled applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), with internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; so too, he reflects that this concentration is rightly awakened and rightly arisen.
When all things have been rightly trained in and rightly arisen, he knows them all to be impermanent and subject to cessation, knowing and seeing them as they truly are, and thus abandons them.

All outflows (āsrava) are liberated from the mind. Although they have not yet severed all outflows, because of their desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, they sever the five lower categories of afflictions (kleśa), are born there by transformation, and attain parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
This is called the second liberation.
Third: When the practitioner, having abandoned rapture (*prīti*), dwells in equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindful (*smṛta*) and clearly conscious (*saṃprajānan*),
experiences with the body that bliss (*sukha*) which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss," and thus accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna—

thus reflecting upon this concentration, training correctly, and generating it correctly— if, after having trained correctly and generated it correctly in all respects, he fully knows it to be impermanent and subject to cessation, then...
Through true knowledge and vision, one abandons all outflows (*āsrava*), and the mind attains liberation.

Although the outflows have not yet been entirely severed, because of the desire for the Dharma and the delight in the Dharma, one abandons the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) and is reborn by transformation (*upapāduka*) there to attain parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world. This is called the third liberation.
Fourth: Just as a practitioner abandons pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, dwells in equanimity and mindfulness, purified,
and accomplishes the practice of the fourth dhyāna— thus reflecting that this concentration is rightly awakened and rightly arisen—
if all [factors] are rightly trained and rightly arisen, one fully knows them to be impermanent and subject to cessation, knowing and seeing them as they truly are, and thereby abandons them.

All outflows (āsrava) are liberated from the mind. Although they have not yet severed all outflows, because of their desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, they sever the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), are reborn by transformation there, and attain parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
This is the fourth liberation.

Fifth: Just as a practitioner extends a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) throughout the four quarters, above, and below—this entire mind of loving-kindness being vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill-will—and thus contemplates this mind of loving-kindness, training correctly and generating it correctly;
if one has fully known that all such correct training and generation have ceased, this is impermanence and cessation.
He knows and sees the Dharma as it truly is; he abandons all outflows (āsrava) and his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet abandoned all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, he severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn there by transformation, and attains parinirvāṇa.
Not returning to this world—this is the fifth liberation.
The sixth refers to the practitioner’s mind of compassionate liberation pervading the four directions, above, and below; it is the mind of universal compassionate liberation.
Vast, supreme, non-dual, and immeasurable; without enmity and without ill will—thus one contemplates this mind of compassionate liberation.

One trains correctly and generates it correctly. When all such correct training and generation have been completed, one knows them fully as impermanent and subject to cessation, seeing and knowing them as they truly are.
One cuts off all outflows (*āsrava*) and the mind attains liberation. Even if one has not yet cut off all outflows, [one remains thus].

Because of their desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, they sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), are reborn there by transformation (*upapāduka*), and attain parinirvāṇa without returning to this world. This is called the sixth liberation.
Seventh, the mind of joy (*muditā-citta*).
Eighth, the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), both of which are the same as before and without difference.

Ninth, it refers to the practitioner who is free from all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and has extinguished perceptions of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃjñā*), and does not direct his thoughts toward...

The perception of diversity (*nānatta-saññā*). What is meant by the perception of diversity? It refers to the various sentient beings, the various objects, the various spheres of experience, the various purities, and the various afflictions;

these are called the perception of diversity. Having attained the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), one enters this meditative absorption through such reflection, training correctly and giving rise [to it] correctly.
When all that has been correctly trained in and correctly produced is exhausted, one knows it to be impermanent.
One knows and sees the dharma of cessation as it truly is; all outflows (*āsrava*) are severed, and the mind attains liberation.

Although the outflows have not yet been entirely severed, because of the desire for the Dharma and the delight in the Dharma, one severs the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), is reborn there by transformation (*upapāduka*), and attains *parinirvāṇa* without returning to this world. This is called the ninth liberation.
Tenth: This refers to the practitioner who, having departed from the sphere of infinite space, accomplishes the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Thus reflecting, he enters this meditative absorption; he trains correctly and gives rise [to it] correctly.

When all such correct training and correct arising have been fully known, he knows and sees as it truly is that these are impermanent and subject to cessation. He abandons all taints, and his mind attains liberation.
Although they have not yet severed all outflows (*āsrava*), because of their desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, they sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
They are reborn there by transformation and attain parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world. This is the tenth liberation.
Eleventh: This refers to the practitioner who, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, achieves the practice of the sphere of nothingness.
Thus reflecting, they enter this meditative absorption, training correctly and giving rise to it correctly.

When all such correct training and correct arising have been fully known, they know and see as it truly is that these are impermanent and subject to cessation; they sever all outflows, and their mind attains liberation.

Liberated. Although he has not yet severed all outflows (*āsrava*), because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, he severs the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and is reborn by transformation (*upapāduka*) there to attain *parinirvāṇa*, never returning to this world. This is called the eleventh liberation.
Twelfth: This refers to the practitioner who, having transcended all the sphere of nothingness, achieves the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus contemplating, he enters this meditative absorption; he trains correctly and is born therein.

When all that is rightly awakened and rightly produced has been exhausted, he knows it as impermanent and subject to cessation, knowing and seeing it as it truly is. He abandons all taints (*āsrava*). His mind...

One attains liberation. Although one has not yet severed all outflows (*āsrava*), because of the desire for the Dharma and the joy of the Dharma, one severs the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) and is reborn by transformation there (*upapāduka*) to attain parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
This is the twelfth liberation. Just as a person seeking one treasure-trove finds eleven, so too, seeking one liberation, one enters [the path].
One attains the eleven liberations. It is like entering the house of an elder which has eleven doors;
though it is being consumed by fire with fierce and blazing flames, when the elder and his sons desire to exit, they are able to leave through any of the doors at their own will.
The practitioner is also like this: within the eleven dharma-doors, wherever one wishes to exit, one attains it according to one's intent.
Upon emerging, one should seek a single liberation; having attained eleven liberations, they are thus called the "eleven liberations.
Among these eleven branches of the path, by cultivating even a single dharma, one attains the fruit of the path; it does not mean that all dharmas must be cultivated in their entirety.
Thus one attains liberation; hence it is said that "from the path of a single factor" up to "the path of eleven factors.
*Yun* (殞) is pronounced *yun*; it means to die.
Regarding the precept against great falsehood, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this world, among the sentient beings of the six realms of existence... and so forth.
"Samādhi does not attain purity," and so forth. Samādhi is also called samāpatti; this is translated as "equanimous concentration" (等持).
It refers to the application of skillful means according to conditions, wherein one brings the mind to rest within conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All meditative concentrations that collect the mind are termed samādhi. In the language of Qin, it is called "the sphere of right mental activity. This mind arises from the... [text continues].

When it first arrives, it is always curved and not straight; once this mind has attained rectitude, its course becomes upright and direct. It is like a snake that moves in constant curves, yet becomes straight when entering a bamboo tube.

The fourth fascicle:

Regarding the "five hindrances" (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*), the term "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) carries the meaning of covering or obscuring. This means that by means of these five delusions, such as greed and so forth, the mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) of all sentient beings is covered and obscured;
consequently, they are unable to clearly perceive the Right Path, remain stagnant within the three realms (*tridhātu*), and are unable to [proceed further].
This is renunciation.

First is the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). Regarding "sensual desire": to take up [objects] without satiety is called "greed" (*rāga*); to long for, require, and yearn for them is called "desire" (*chanda*).
This refers to the way all sentient beings greedily crave the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects of the world, as well as material wealth, including both male and female.

Regarding treasures and such things, there is no satiety; by means of this greed and desire, the mind and consciousness are shrouded, such that meditative concentration and wholesome dharmas cannot arise.
One remains stagnant within the three realms and fails to attain liberation; therefore, it is called a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
2. The Hindrance of Ill Will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*). "Ill will" refers to a mind of resentment.
This means that sentient beings, either with respect to disagreeable objects or by recollecting how others have harmed them or their kin, give rise to resentment.
Because of this ill will, the mind and consciousness are shrouded; thus, the wholesome dharmas of meditative concentration cannot arise, and one remains stagnant.
Because one cannot achieve liberation from the three realms, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

Third is the hindrance of sleep (*middha-nīvaraṇa*). Regarding "sleep": the dulling and maturing of the mental consciousness is called "sleep" (*svapna*); the darkening and obscuration of the five sensory faculties is called "slumber" (*middha*).
As for the "five sensory faculties," these are the five organs of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. This refers to all sentient beings.
Because this sleep covers and obscures the mind and consciousness, the wholesome dharmas of meditative concentration cannot arise;
one remains stagnant within the three realms with no prospect of escape. Therefore, it is called a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).

The fourth is the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*). Regarding "restlessness and remorse": "restlessness" (*auddhatya*) refers to agitation. When the body wanders about without purpose, it is called restlessness;
having become restless, one reflects upon it, and the resulting distress within the mind is remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

It is said that all sentient beings, by means of this restlessness and remorse, shroud their consciousness so that wholesome dharmas such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) cannot arise. They remain stagnant within the three realms, with no prospect of liberation. Therefore—
It is called a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding the five hindrances of doubt: "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) carries the meaning of being hesitant and indecisive; it is precisely what is meant by "perplexity.

This refers to sentient beings who, due to the darkness and dullness of ignorance (*avidyā*), cannot distinguish between the true and the false; their state of hesitation is constantly unresolved. Because of this—

Doubt and uncertainty shroud the mind-consciousness, preventing the arising of wholesome dharmas such as meditative concentration. One remains stagnant within the three realms with no prospect of escape;
therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
The *Śrāvastī-madhyama-pañcakāmaguṇa-śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not themselves desire;

rather, they possess flavors that can give rise to the desirous mind in the practitioner. Therefore, they are called the 'five desires. They are so named because they constantly draw people into the realms of Māra."

First, desire for form (*rūpa-rāga*): this refers to the handsome features of men and women, as well as various exquisite colors such as black, yellow, red, and purple among the world’s precious objects;
because these can cause sentient beings to delight in them and become attached without satiety, it is called desire for form.
Second is the desire for sounds (*śabdakāma*): this refers to the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, jade ornaments, and the like, as well as the sounds of men and women singing and chanting.
Because these can cause sentient beings to become attached with delight and never grow weary, they are called the desire for sounds.
Third, the desire for fragrance (*gandha-kāma*): this refers to the bodily fragrance of men and women, as well as all worldly fragrances.
Because they cause sentient beings to delight in them and become attached without satiety, it is called the desire for fragrance.
Fourth, the desire for flavors (*rasa-kāma*): this refers to various delicious foods, drinks, delicacies, and so forth, which cause sentient beings to delight in them and never grow weary;
therefore, it is called the desire for flavors.
Fifth, the desire for touch (*spraṣṭavya-kāma*): this refers to the softness and smoothness of the bodies of men and women, as well as their warmth when it is cold and [coolness] when it is hot.

A cool sensation, as well as various pleasant tactile objects such as clothing and the like, which cause sentient beings to delight in them and never tire of doing so—this is called the desire for touch (*spraṣṭavya-kāma*).
The character *yào* (鑰) is pronounced *yào*; it refers to keys and locks, the tools used for opening and closing locks.

Wòrǎng (upper tone wù; lower tone ráng): "Wò" refers to a spring that flows downward from above.
"Rǎng" refers to soft soil without clods. This "rǎng" is red earth from which all things grow spontaneously, such that it does not require irrigation.

Volume five: *Dǐ* (羝). The sound is *dī*. A three-year-old ram is called a *dǐ*. Its nature is to butt.
"Pliant forbearance" (*kṣānti*) refers to Mañjuśrī preaching the Dharma to them.

"The mind attaining pliancy through repentance" means that regarding both principle and phenomena, one is able to accord with them, thoroughly examining and accepting them without opposition or contradiction. This is what is meant by "forbearance."
The Piṇḍala Hell is here called the "Desire-Cloud. Upon entering, one immediately exits; although one remains within it, there is no suffering.
One attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The patience of non-arising refers to the thorough realization that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen. Furthermore...
There is no cessation; one should examine this with truth and accept it with patience, so that deluded thoughts do not arise.
The twelvefold teaching is also called the twelvefold scripture: first, *sūtra*—in the language of China, this means "scripture of agreement" (*jìngīng*).
"Sūtra" (Kie) means that, above, it accords with the principle of all Buddhas; below, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

"Sūtra" (Jing) refers to the threading together of the explained meanings and principles so that they are not lost, and the gathering and sustaining of those to be converted so that their capacities do not fall away.
This refers to the prose sections within the sūtras; hence, it is called *sūtra* (Kie-jing).
2. Geya: In the language of China, this means "Verses in Response" (Ying-song) or "Repetitive Verses" (Chong-song). It refers to verses that restate the meaning of prose passages (gadya).
3. Gāthā: In the language of China, this means "Recited Verses" (Feng-song). It refers to verses that do not restate prose, but are spoken directly as metrical stanzas.
The four *nidānas* (in Chinese, *yīnyuán*, "causes and conditions") refer to instances such as when someone asks a question in a sutra, and the Buddha consequently explains this matter;
or when someone commits an offense in accordance with the Vinaya, and the Buddha consequently establishes this precept.
All fundamental accounts of the origins of events spoken by the Tathāgata are termed *nidāna*. An example is found in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This refers to the accounts of past lives and so forth.

Fifth is *itivṛttaka*, which in the language of China is called "Past Deeds" (*benshi*). This refers to the narration of the deeds performed by various bodhisattvas and disciples during their stages as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
As stated in the "Chapter on Past Deeds" (*Itivṛttaka-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, at sunrise..."
This refers to how, in the presence of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he attained joy in the Dharma and immediately offered his own body and arms as an act of worship,
practicing various ascetic disciplines and seeking the path to Bodhi.
Sixth, *jātaka* (in the language of the Flower [China], "Birth Story"). This refers to accounts of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas taking birth in their previous states.

As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bhikṣus, you should know that in the past I was a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, a dragon, and even a *suvarṇa*-scattering king or a *cakravartin* wheel-turning sage king; such are my various forms."
*Abhūta-dharma*: in the language of China, this means "unprecedented" or "rare. It refers, for example, to when the Buddha was first born, he immediately took seven steps;
at the places where his footprints fell, lotus flowers appeared, and he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, uttering these words:
"I am the one who shall deliver all sentient beings from birth, old age, and sickness."
When one dies, the earth shakes violently, the heavens rain down various flowers, trees produce sounds, and celestial music is played;
such are these immeasurable and rare wonders.
*Avadāna*: Fully rendered as *Apadāna*, translated into Chinese as "Parable" (*pìyù*).
This refers to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma for those of dull faculties by employing parables to instruct and enlighten them, thereby enabling them to attain understanding.
An example is found in the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), such as the parables of the burning house and the medicinal herbs.
Ninth, the *upadeśa* (instructional treatises), which are discursive expositions consisting of questions, answers, and debates concerning the various dharmas within the sūtras.

An example is the discussion between the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa and Mañjuśrī regarding the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as found in the "Devadatta" chapter. In Sanskrit, *Devadatta*; in Chinese: [Devadatta].
The weather is hot. In Sanskrit, Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) in Chinese.

*Udāna*—meaning "Spontaneous Utterance" (Zishuo) in Chinese—refers to those teachings which the Tathāgata proclaims on his own initiative without anyone having asked him, as he perceives the capacities of sentient beings through his knowledge of others' minds.
This is like the account of the fifty kinds of demons spoken of at the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly.

Matter. It does not depend upon Ānanda’s inquiry. Regarding the fifty kinds of māras: this refers to the five aggregates (skandhas)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—each of which has ten types.

Regarding *pratyeka*: in the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *pratyekabuddha*; in the language of China, it means "enlightened by conditions" (*yuanjue*).

"Hào-táo" (號咷): the upper character is pronounced *háo* and the lower character is pronounced *táo*;

*Huì* (huì) [with the third tone]: wealth. Gold and jade are called *huò* (goods); cloth and silk are called *huì*.
Regarding the four *saṃgraha-vastu* (means of integration), these four are collectively termed "integration" (*shè*). "Integration" (*shè*) means to receive and embrace (*shèshòu*).

This means that when a Bodhisattva wishes to transform and guide sentient beings, they must necessarily integrate them by means of these four methods to cause them to rely [on the Bodhisattva], and only then can they be guided.
By means of the true path of the Mahāyāna, as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "First one entices with the hook of desire, and later causes entry into the Buddha-wisdom.
First is gathering through giving (*dāna*): this refers to the Bodhisattva gathering sentient beings through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma.
If sentient beings delight in material wealth, one gathers them in by means of the gift of wealth; if sentient beings delight in the Dharma, one gathers them in by means of the gift of the Dharma.

Once sentient beings have received the benefit of these two gifts, they consequently give rise to affection and love, relying upon [the teacher] to receive the Path and attaining abiding in the True Principle. Therefore, this is called gathering through giving.

Second is the inclusion through pleasant speech (*priyavāditā-saṃgraha*). This means that when a bodhisattva accords with the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings and consoles them with virtuous words, all sentient beings delight in hearing those virtuous words;
consequently, they give rise to affection and love, relying upon [the bodhisattva] to receive the Path and attain abiding in the True Principle.
Therefore, it is called the inclusion through pleasant speech.
The inclusion by means of beneficial conduct (*hitacaryā-saṃgraha*): This refers to the bodhisattva’s cultivation of wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind to benefit all sentient beings.

Because of this, [sentient beings] give rise to affection and love, rely [upon the bodhisattva], receive the path, and attain abiding in the true reality; therefore, it is called inclusion by means of beneficial conduct.
Fourth, the integration through common purpose (*samānārthatā-saṃgraha*). This means that the Bodhisattva, with the eye of Dharma, clearly perceives the faculties and natures of sentient beings.
According to their inclinations, he manifests various forms and engages in the same activities as they do, so that each may receive benefit.

Regarding the five desires (*pañca-kāma*), the first is the desire for wealth (*dhana-kāma*). "Wealth" refers to all worldly assets and resources.

This means that because people rely on material goods as the means for their own sustenance, they fall into greedy seeking and become attached to them without relinquishing them; this constitutes the desire for wealth.
Second is the desire for form (*rūpa-rāga*). Form refers to the worldly colors of blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as the forms of male and female and so forth.
Because people find pleasure and satisfaction in these forms, they come to greedily seek them and become attached to them, thereby being unable to escape the three realms (*tridhātu*).
This is the desire for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*).
Third is the desire for food and drink (*āhāra-tṛṣṇā*); "food and drink" refers to the various flavors of worldly delicacies.

This means that humans must rely on food and drink to sustain the body and maintain life; therefore, they greedily seek them out with attachment and never find satiety. This is the desire for food and drink.
The fourth is the desire for fame (*nāma-kāma*). "Fame" refers to worldly reputation. This means that because people rely on reputation, they can manifest their kinship and honor themselves;
thus, they pursue it with greed and attachment, not knowing when to stop. This is called the desire for fame.
Fifth, the desire for sleep: sleep refers to the state where the mental consciousness becomes clouded and one slumbers.
This means that even human sleep has its proper seasons; if one is indolent, negligent, or indulgent, and takes pleasure in it without satiety, this constitutes the desire for sleep.
